Article Title: Connecticut student Raji Doshi, 12, designed an algae and calcium system to reduce ocean acidity; she is now competing for a $25,000 science prize
Article Text:
Raji Doshi (Image Credit: Young Scientist Lab)

A project inspired by a global environmental challenge

How the proposed system works

A chance to showcase young scientific talent

A 12-year-old student from Connecticut is drawing attention for tackling one of the world's biggest environmental challenges with an innovative science project. According to the Young Scientist Lab, Raji Doshi designed a project that proposes using algae and natural calcium (aragonite) buffers to help reduce CO₂-driven ocean acidification. Her innovative idea has earned her a place among this year's finalists, where she is now competing for the competition's $25,000 grand prize.Ocean acidification is a major concern for scientists because the world's oceans absorb a significant amount of the carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere. As more carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, the water becomes more acidic, making it harder for corals, shellfish and other marine organisms to build and maintain their shells and skeletons.According to her finalist profile on the Young Scientist Lab website, Raji's project explores whether combining algae with natural calcium (aragonite) buffers can help counter this process. The idea is based on the natural ability of algae to absorb carbon dioxide during photosynthesis, while calcium compounds may help buffer acidity by increasing the water's alkalinity.Rather than relying on a single solution, her project investigates how these two natural processes could work together to create healthier conditions for marine ecosystems.According to Raji's project summary, the proposed system uses natural calcium (aragonite) buffers, which may help counter rising acidity by increasing seawater alkalinity. Since carbon dioxide is one of the main drivers of ocean acidification, reducing its concentration could help slow changes in seawater chemistry.By combining algae with natural calcium (aragonite) buffers, the proposed approach aims to create a more balanced aquatic environment that could benefit marine organisms vulnerable to acidic conditions. The project explores how these biological and chemical processes could work together to help reduce the impacts of ocean acidification.While the project is still a student research initiative rather than a commercially tested technology, it reflects an innovative approach to addressing a complex environmental issue. It also demonstrates how scientific concepts from biology and chemistry can be combined to explore practical solutions to real-world problems.Raji's project has secured her a place among the finalists in the 2026 3M Young Scientist Challenge, a competition that recognises young innovators for developing creative solutions to important global issues.As a finalist, she will present her work before a panel of judges while competing for the $25,000 top prize. The competition also gives participants an opportunity to receive mentorship, refine their ideas and gain recognition for their scientific research.Although the outcome of the competition is yet to be decided, Raji's selection as a finalist highlights the growing role that young students can play in environmental innovation. Her project encourages discussion about sustainable approaches to protecting marine ecosystems while demonstrating how curiosity and scientific thinking can inspire new ideas.By focusing on ocean acidification, a challenge affecting oceans around the world, Raji's project illustrates how young researchers are increasingly contributing fresh perspectives to some of today's most pressing environmental issues. Whether her proposed system ultimately leads to further research or inspires future innovations, her work reflects the power of science education in encouraging the next generation of problem-solvers.
Article Summary: Raji Doshi, 12, is a finalist in the 2026 3M Young Scientist Challenge. Her project proposes using algae and natural calcium (aragonite) buffers to help reduce CO₂-driven ocean acidification. She is now competing for the competition's $25,000 grand prize.

Article Title: Meet the General Grant Tree: The world's second-largest tree that became America's only living National Shrine
Article Text:
PC: wikipedia

General Grant Tree size: How tall is the world's second-largest tree



How the General Grant Tree became America's National Christmas Tree



Why the General Grant Tree is America's only living National Shrine



Why the General Grant Tree remains one of California's greatest natural landmarks



Most people who have heard of giant sequoias can usually name one tree: the General Sherman Tree. Far fewer realise that another extraordinary giant stands only a short distance away in California's Sequoia and Kings Canyon National Parks. The General Grant Tree does not hold the title of the world's largest tree, yet its dimensions remain difficult to grasp even when standing beneath it. Beyond its sheer size, it has accumulated a remarkable public history over the past century. It has become the United States' National Christmas Tree, the country's only living National Shrine, and an enduring symbol that blends natural history with national remembrance. Together, those distinctions make it unlike any other tree on Earth.The General Grant Tree is a giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) growing in Grant Grove within Kings Canyon National Park in California. Although it is widely recognised as the second-largest tree on Earth when measured by trunk volume, that description only hints at its scale.According to the US National Park Service, the tree stands 268.1 feet (81.7 metres) tall.Around its base, the trunk measures 107.5 feet (32.8 metres) in circumference and contains an estimated 46,608 cubic feet (1,320 cubic metres) of wood.Looking upward from the trail, visitors often struggle to judge its height because the immense trunk continues almost uninterrupted before disappearing into a dense canopy high above the forest floor. The experience simply: "It is difficult to comprehend the immense size, age and stature of the General Grant Tree, but it is easy to let your mind and spirit rise as its trunk carries your gaze toward the skies."A short paved loop of roughly one-third of a mile leads visitors to the tree while also passing other features of Grant Grove, including the Fallen Monarch, the Gamlin Cabin and the Centennial Stump.As per the US National Park Service, the tree's cultural story began with an unexpectedly ordinary moment. In 1924, Californian visitor R.J. Senior was standing beside the General Grant Tree with a young girl when she remarked, "What a wonderful Christmas tree it would be!" The comment stayed with him.Working alongside Charles E. Lee, Senior organised a Christmas gathering beneath the giant sequoia the following year. The ceremony was held at noon on Christmas Day in 1925, establishing a tradition that continues nearly a century later.Their efforts eventually reached the White House. On 28 April 1926, President Calvin Coolidge officially designated the General Grant Tree as the Nation's Christmas Tree.Annual celebrations continued through changing times and difficult winters. National Park Service records describe people travelling through snow, returning year after year, and in one instance making the journey even after heavy snowfall forced the official ceremony outside the park. Rangers still placed the traditional wreath beneath the tree, preserving the custom despite the conditions. The annual "Trek to the Tree", organised by the Sanger Chamber of Commerce, continues each December.The General Grant Tree gained another unique role three decades after receiving its Christmas designation. In 1956, President Dwight D. Eisenhower declared it a National Shrine dedicated to "the men and women of the Armed Forces who have served and fought and died to keep this Nation free..."Unlike traditional monuments built from stone or metal, this memorial is alive. The National Park Service states that it remains the only living shrine in the United States.During the dedication ceremony, Fleet Admiral Chester Nimitz compared its significance with one of America's best-known memorials, describing it as having "equal stature with that other great shrine in Arlington Cemetery, the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier." That combination of ecological importance and national remembrance gives the tree a role unlike any other giant sequoia.Grant Grove contains many impressive giant sequoias, but the General Grant Tree naturally draws the greatest attention. Nearby walking routes continue through the grove, passing additional mature trees, open meadows and seasonal streams before connecting with longer trails into surrounding wilderness.Travellers exploring California's sequoia parks often compare the General Grant Tree with the nearby General Sherman Tree in Sequoia National Park. Sherman remains the largest known tree on Earth by trunk volume, while Grant occupies second place.Even without holding the top ranking, the General Grant Tree represents something broader than size alone. Over generations, it has become woven into annual public ceremonies, military remembrance and the shared history of one of America's oldest protected landscapes. Few living organisms combine those roles while continuing to grow quietly in the same place where visitors have gathered for more than a hundred years.
Article Summary: The General Grant Tree is a giant sequoia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) growing in Grant Grove within Kings Canyon National Park in California. According to the US National Park Service, the tree stands 268.1 feet (81.7 metres) tall. The trunk measures 107.5 feet (32.8 metres) in circumference and contains an estimated 46,608 cubic feet (1,320 cubic metres) of wood.

Article Title: Researchers tracked wildfires from 1984 to 2022; a Pacific trend added 22% to US Southwest drying-related burned area but reduced eastern Australia’s by about 19%
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Decades of data reveal a climate connection

Atmospheric dryness is the key

Image Credit: Canva

Opposite wildfire impacts

Improving future wildfire forecasts

A long-term shift in the tropical Pacific Ocean has played contrasting roles in wildfire activity on opposite sides of the world, amplifying fire-prone conditions in the southwestern United States while easing them in eastern Australia. According to a new study published in the journal Nature Communications, the Pacific Ocean pattern increased drying-related burned forest area in the U.S. Southwest by about 22%, but reduced it by roughly 19% in eastern Australia. The findings are based on nearly four decades of wildfire and climate data spanning 1984 to 2022.For the study, researchers analysed satellite observations of burned forest area alongside climate records and advanced climate model simulations covering 39 years. Their goal was to understand how a persistent warming pattern in the tropical Pacific Ocean has influenced wildfire risk in two of the world's most fire-prone regions.Since the 1980s, the western tropical Pacific has warmed faster than the eastern Pacific. This uneven warming alters large-scale atmospheric circulation, influencing rainfall, temperature and humidity far beyond the Pacific through climate teleconnections.The researchers investigated how this long-term oceanic trend interacts with human-driven climate change to affect wildfire conditions.Instead of focusing only on rising temperatures, the team examined vapour pressure deficit (VPD), a measure of atmospheric dryness that indicates how strongly the atmosphere draws moisture from plants and soils. Higher VPD leaves vegetation drier and more susceptible to burning, making it one of the strongest indicators of annual wildfire activity.The researchers used attribution analyses combining observations and climate model simulations to separate the effects of anthropogenic warming from the Pacific Ocean trend. It turned out that although man-made global warming is still the main factor responsible for rising atmospheric dryness, the Pacific signal may either amplify or dampen its impacts.The study found that the Pacific Ocean trend strengthened drying conditions in the southwestern United States, contributing an additional 22% to the increase in burned forest area linked to atmospheric drying. This occurred on top of the strong influence of human-caused warming, which has already driven dramatic increases in wildfire activity across the region.During the study period, burned forest area increased by more than 3,000% in the interior Southwest and by over 1,000% in a coastal region that includes much of California. While global warming accounted for most of this increase, the Pacific Ocean pattern further amplified wildfire-favourable conditions.Eastern Australia experienced the opposite effect. Although climate change also increased atmospheric dryness there, the Pacific trend partially offset that drying, resulting in an estimated 19% reduction in burned forest area compared with what would have been expected from global warming alone.The researchers caution that this does not mean wildfire risk has disappeared in eastern Australia. Rather, the Pacific Ocean pattern temporarily moderated the influence of climate change during the study period.According to the researchers, the findings demonstrate that regional wildfire risk is shaped by both long-term climate change and natural climate variability. While greenhouse gas-driven warming continues to increase atmospheric dryness globally, ocean-driven climate patterns can significantly alter how those impacts are expressed in different regions.Understanding these interactions could improve both seasonal and long-term wildfire forecasting, enabling scientists and policy makers to predict the fire risks in the future. The researchers note that Pacific-driven climate variability influences weather patterns across many parts of the world, suggesting that similar interactions between ocean conditions and human-driven climate change could affect wildfire risk in other regions as well.
Article Summary: Pacific Ocean pattern increased drying-related burned forest area in the U.S. Southwest by about 22%, but reduced it by roughly 19% in eastern Australia. The findings are based on nearly four decades of wildfire and climate data spanning 1984 to 2022. understanding these interactions could improve both seasonal and long-term wildfire forecasting.

Article Title: Scientists solve the 100-year-old mystery behind why avocado flowers change sex over two days
Article Text:
Image(s): Wikipedia

Every avocado flower opens twice, first as a female and then as a male

A single gene controls a rhythm that growers have observed for generations

The unusual flowering pattern helps prevent self-pollination

DNA testing could allow breeders to identify flowering types years earlier

For more than a century, avocado growers have known that not all avocado trees flower in the same way. Some trees produce flowers that function as females in the morning before becoming males the following afternoon, while others follow the opposite schedule. This unusual rhythm has long shaped how orchards are planted, with growers pairing different flowering types to maximise pollination and fruit production. Although the pattern has been carefully documented for generations, the genetic mechanism behind it remained unknown. Now, researchers from the University of California, Davis and the University of California, Riverside have identified a single gene that controls this remarkable flowering cycle, solving one of the oldest mysteries in avocado biology and offering breeders a powerful new tool for developing improved varieties.The findings come from the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) study ‘ Balanced Polymorphism in a Floral Transcription Factor Underlies the Ancient Rhythm of Daily Sex Alternation in Avocado ’ by J.S. Groh and colleagues.Unlike most flowering plants, each avocado flower opens twice over two consecutive days. During its first opening, the flower functions only as a female, capable of receiving pollen but not releasing it. It then closes for the night before reopening the following day as a male, releasing pollen after its female phase has ended.This sequence occurs in every flower, but entire trees follow one of two distinct schedules. A-type trees open their flowers as females in the morning and reopen as males the following afternoon. B-type trees do exactly the reverse, beginning their female phase in the afternoon before becoming male the following morning.To uncover the genetic basis of this unusual flowering pattern, the researchers sequenced the genomes of hundreds of avocado trees representing both flowering types.Their analyses traced the entire difference to a single gene known as SDMYB, a floral transcription factor that switches on a network of other genes responsible for coordinating when flowers open, close and transition between female and male phases.The study found that a dominant version of the gene produces A-type flowering, while a recessive version results in B-type trees. Rather than involving dozens of interacting genes, one genetic difference appears to determine the flowering schedule that growers have relied upon for decades.to Groh and colleagues, this provides a remarkably simple explanation for a biological phenomenon that has puzzled botanists and avocado breeders for around 100 years.The research also explains why the two flowering types are so important for successful avocado production.If every flower on every tree became female and male at exactly the same time, opportunities for pollen transfer between trees would be greatly reduced. Instead, the alternating schedules ensure that female-phase flowers on one tree overlap with male-phase flowers on another, maintaining a continuous supply of pollen throughout the day.This staggered timing encourages cross-pollination rather than self-fertilisation, increasing the likelihood of successful fruit production. It is also why commercial orchards have traditionally planted both A-type and B-type cultivars together, even before the underlying genetics were understood.One of the most practical outcomes of the discovery concerns avocado breeding. At present, breeders often have to wait several years before a young avocado tree matures and produces its first flowers, allowing its flowering type to be identified through observation.Because the new study links flowering behaviour directly to the SDMYB gene, breeders can now determine whether a seedling will become an A-type or B-type tree using a simple DNA test, long before the plant reaches maturity.The researchers suggest this could significantly accelerate breeding programmes by allowing desirable flowering combinations to be selected much earlier, saving both time and resources.By identifying the genetic switch behind avocado flowering, J.S. Groh and colleagues have solved one of horticulture's longest-standing puzzles. Their discovery not only explains why avocado flowers change from female to male over two days but also provides growers and breeders with a practical genetic tool that could improve orchard planning and speed the development of future avocado varieties.
Article Summary: Every avocado flower opens twice, first as a female and then as a male. A-type trees open their flowers as females in the morning and reopen as males the following afternoon. B- type trees do exactly the reverse, beginning their female phase in the afternoon before becoming male the following morning. This unusual rhythm has long shaped how orchards are planted.

Article Title: Nearly 81 years after Hiroshima, scientists discover a hidden metal alloy created by the atomic bomb blast
Article Text:
image AI generated

How the new Hiroshima metal alloy was discovered in beach sand samples



How the Hiroshima atomic bomb blast created the new metal alloy



Why the new Hiroshima metal alloy could help future materials science research



How Hiroshima atomic bomb debris could help scientists study past nuclear explosions



Nearly 81 years after the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, material recovered from the city's shoreline is still yielding discoveries that scientists did not expect. Researchers examining tiny fragments preserved in beach sands have identified what appears to be a previously unknown metallic alloy that formed during the immense heat and rapid cooling triggered by the 6 August 1945 explosion.The finding is less about rewriting the history of the bombing than expanding what scientists know about how matter behaves under conditions that are almost impossible to recreate. According to a new study published in Science Advances, titled “ Discovery of a multicomponent alloy forged by the Hiroshima atomic blast ”, the alloy developed inside microscopic particles known as "hiroshimaites", offering researchers an unusual glimpse into how extreme temperatures, vaporised building materials and rapid solidification combined to produce a material that has not previously been documented.The newly identified alloy was discovered during an examination of 34 Hiroshimaite samples collected from Hiroshima Bay. While most of the metallic particles consisted of familiar iron-chromium-based alloys, one grain stood apart because of its unusually high silicon content and its distinctive chemical makeup.According to the researchers, the microscopic fragment contains iron, chromium, nickel, manganese, molybdenum, silicon and small amounts of aluminium arranged in a combination unlike previously reported natural or industrial alloys.Laboratory analysis showed that the particle was chemically uniform, suggesting it crystallised from a single molten droplet before cooling so rapidly that its internal structure remained locked in place.The team also determined that the alloy crystallised in an ordered AlAu₄-type crystal structure, a configuration that differs from the body-centred cubic or face-centred cubic structures commonly associated with stainless-steel-like materials.The atomic airburst generated temperatures exceeding 7,000°C within seconds, vaporising metals, concrete, soil, glass and other urban materials into an expanding fireball. As that cloud cooled, different elements condensed from the mixed vapour and rapidly solidified into microscopic droplets.The researchers suggest that the newly discovered alloy most likely formed through this sequence of vaporisation, condensation and ultrafast quenching rather than existing before the explosion. They also argue that its chemical composition and crystal structure do not match known industrial alloys, making it unlikely that the particle simply survived the blast intact.These fireball conditions are a rare natural environment where entirely new metallic phases can emerge because the cooling process happens too quickly for atoms to arrange themselves into the structures normally seen during conventional metal production.Although the alloy itself is not expected to become an engineering material, researchers believe it could help broaden understanding of complex multicomponent alloys. These materials are already of interest because certain compositions can combine strength, corrosion resistance and thermal stability in ways that conventional alloys cannot.The Hiroshima particle provides a real-world example of how extreme environments can stabilise unusual crystal structures that may inspire future laboratory research. They emphasise that the discovery points towards unexplored regions of alloy design rather than an immediately practical material.Earlier investigations of debris from the Trinity nuclear test identified an unusual quasicrystal formed under similar extreme conditions. The newly described Hiroshima alloy does not belong to the same category, but the researchers say both findings suggest nuclear fireballs can generate structures that rarely form through conventional geological or industrial processes.Beyond materials science, the researchers argue that blast-derived particles may preserve detailed records of the conditions present during nuclear explosions. By analysing their chemistry, crystal structure and formation history, scientists may gain a better understanding of the temperatures, mixing processes and cooling rates that occurred during such events.Atomic-blast debris acts as an unintended record of extreme physical processes, preserving microscopic materials that could otherwise never have formed. The authors suggest that continued, carefully managed scientific examination of these particles may contribute both to future materials research and to nuclear forensics, while also offering new insight into one of the most significant events of the twentieth century.
Article Summary: Researchers examining tiny fragments preserved in beach sands have identified what appears to be a previously unknown metallic alloy. The finding is less about rewriting the history of the bombing than expanding what scientists know about how matter behaves under conditions that are almost impossible to recreate.

Article Title: Mississippi man uncovers more than 200 Civil War cannonballs buried beneath his property after 160 years
Article Text:
Image: WTVA 9 News/YouTube

A routine excavation uncovered one of Mississippi's largest Civil War ordnance discoveries

Bomb disposal experts were called because some cannonballs could still be dangerous

The cache may have been buried during military activity more than 160 years ago

Civil War discoveries continue to emerge beneath American soil

What began as an ordinary day of digging on private land in Mississippi turned into one of the state's most remarkable Civil War discoveries in recent years. While working on his property, a local resident uncovered what initially appeared to be a handful of rusted iron spheres. As excavation continued, the number kept growing until more than 200 Civil War-era cannonballs emerged from the ground. The cache, buried for over 160 years, is believed to date back to the American Civil War, offering a rare glimpse into one of the conflict's most turbulent periods. The discovery also prompted an urgent response from explosives experts, as some of the projectiles still had the potential to contain explosive material despite spending more than a century underground.The discovery was made by Bobby Boyette on his Mississippi property, as he was conducting excavations, and the workers started to unearth massive iron balls underground.According to The New York Post, it all started as a single discovery that eventually became much bigger. While digging, more and more cannonballs were found in the same place until they amounted to over 200, leaving everyone involved surprised.Considering the age and nature of these items, officials determined that these were the cannonballs of Civil War times, which took place between 1861 and 1865.Even though more than a century and a half had gone by since the Civil War, the finding was handled with utmost caution.It is for this reason that the explosive ordnance disposal team was summoned to examine the find because some old cannon balls can still be explosive even if they have not been fired.This means that the experts had to examine the old balls to find out whether there were solid iron shot and which could still be explosive.Even though the real cause for the burials of the cannonballs is unknown, historians believe that they most probably came into being due to warfare in the Civil War times in Mississippi.There were many battles and military operations conducted in Mississippi at that time, and armies moved around carrying gunpowder supplies in the state. Some of the gunpowder supplies could have been left behind as well.According to the New York Post, there is such a quantity of cannonballs found that it is possible that they used to be part of the supply.Over 160 years after the end of the Civil War, archaeological finds still keep on uncovering hidden remains of the war in America.Objects such as bullets, artillery, weaponry, and even private belongings are found from time to time while working on farms, construction projects, and excavation works, allowing historians to learn a lot about the troops' locations during the war. What makes the Mississippi discovery unique is both its magnitude and historical value.Finding more than 200 cannonballs from the period of the Civil War in one spot is quite unusual, giving yet another chance to touch upon one of the most important wars in American history while emphasising the necessity of handling historic military ordnance very carefully even after such a long time underground.
Article Summary: A routine excavation uncovered one of Mississippi's largest Civil War ordnance discoveries. Bomb disposal experts were called because some cannonballs could still be dangerous. The cache, buried for over 160 years, is believed to date back to the American Civil War.

Article Title: Meet Nathan Thomas: 18-year-old Florida teen becomes the world's youngest male professor after breaking a 306-year-old record
Article Text:
How Nathan Thomas became the world's youngest male professor

Image: CBS Miami

An extraordinary academic journey

A passion for engineering and teaching

Looking beyond engineering





An inspiration for young learners

At an age when many students are just beginning university, Nathan Thomas had already stepped into the classroom as a college professor. The Florida native earned a place in the Guinness World Records after becoming the world's youngest male professor at just 18 years and 346 days old, breaking a record that had stood for 306 years. Thomas joined Miami Dade College as an engineering instructor, where he teaches students who are often close to his own age. His remarkable academic journey, which began with enrolling in college at the age of 10, has now made him one of the youngest educators ever to teach at the higher education level.Nathan Thomas officially became the world's youngest male professor when he accepted an engineering teaching position at Miami Dade College at the age of 18 years and 346 days. Guinness World Records confirmed that he surpassed the record previously held by Scottish mathematician Colin Maclaurin, who became a professor at the age of 19 in 1717. The achievement ended a record that had remained unbeaten for more than three centuries.Thomas began teaching COP 2270: C for Engineers at Miami Dade College in August 2023. The course introduces engineering students to the fundamentals of C programming and computational problem-solving.Many of his students are around the same age as him, but Thomas believes age matters far less than a willingness to learn. He has said that everyone enters the classroom with the same goal of gaining knowledge and improving their skills.Thomas displayed exceptional academic ability from an early age. At just 10 years old, he dual-enrolled at Miami Dade College while continuing his school education. By the age of 14, he had transferred to Florida International University, where he completed both bachelor's and master's degrees in electrical engineering with honours. His accelerated academic path eventually led him back to Miami Dade College, this time as a faculty member rather than a student.Coming from a family of engineers, Thomas developed an interest in mathematics and science at a young age. He has credited his mother with helping him understand mathematical concepts in ways that made learning enjoyable. He says the most rewarding part of teaching is watching students grasp ideas that once seemed difficult, describing those moments as just as satisfying as solving engineering problems himself.While continuing to teach, Thomas is also pursuing a Juris Doctor degree at the University of Miami School of Law, with an expected graduation in 2028. He hopes to combine his engineering background with legal expertise by specialising in intellectual property law, particularly in areas involving science, technology, engineering and mathematics. According to Thomas, the structured problem-solving skills he developed through engineering have proved valuable in his legal studies.Nathan Thomas's achievement demonstrates how determination, curiosity and a passion for learning can open extraordinary opportunities at a young age. From entering college as a child to becoming the world's youngest male professor and breaking a 306-year-old Guinness World Record, his journey has inspired students and educators alike. As he continues balancing teaching with law school, Thomas hopes to contribute to both education and innovation while encouraging others to pursue ambitious goals regardless of age.
Article Summary: Nathan Thomas became the world's youngest male professor at the age of 18 years and 346 days. The record was previously held by Scottish mathematician Colin Maclaurin, who was 19 in 1717. Thomas is also pursuing a Juris Doctor degree at the University of Miami School of Law, with an expected graduation in 2028.

Article Title: Russia's overnight ballistic missile and drone attack on Ukraine capital Kyiv kills 9
Article Text:
Fire breaks out at Moscow's St Basil's Cathedral

At least nine people were killed and twenty-eight others were injured after Russia launched a barrage of ballistic missiles and drones targeting Ukraine's capital Kyiv overnight into Saturday. The attack damaged residential buildings, sparked multiple fires across the city and left people trapped under debris, officials said.Kyiv mayor Vitalii Klitschko had earlier said a five-storey residential building in the Solomianskyi district was struck by falling debris, causing severe damage and trapping residents inside."The first and second floors of the damaged residential building had partially collapsed," Klitschko said in a post on Telegram, adding that a fire had also broken out in the courtyard.Klitschko had said at least three people had been killed in the Russian missile attack and confirmed that several people remained trapped in the partially collapsed building. He added that five people had been hospitalised following the strikes.People were also believed to be trapped in another residential building in the Shevchenkivskyi district after the first and second floors partially collapsed, Klitschko said.Additionally, seven people were killed and 14 others injured in Kyiv's Darnytskyi district after the attack sparked fires and damaged homes, vehicles, an administrative building and other non-residential structures, emergency services told news agency AP.According to Reuters witnesses, more than a dozen explosions reverberated across the Ukrainian capital during the attack. This comes as Russia stepped up strikes on Kyiv in recent months, while Ukraine continues to face a shortage of air defence systems capable of intercepting ballistic missiles, which travel several times faster than the speed of sound.The latest bombardment came just two days after another large-scale Russian ballistic missile and drone attack across Ukraine killed 10 civilians and wounded more than 50 others. During that attack, a Russian missile also briefly entered Polish airspace.As Russian aerial attacks intensified, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy reiterated Kyiv's demand for additional Patriot air defence systems from the United States and its Western allies."The Russian air strikes on our country continue and air defense, specifically interceptors for Patriot systems against ballistic missiles, remains a top priority," Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram on Friday.The Ukrainian president also said he had spoken with US vice president JD Vance after his meeting earlier this week in Washington with president Donald Trump.The renewed appeal comes amid uncertainty over future US military support. At the Nato summit in Ankara in July, president Trump said the United States would grant Ukraine a licence to manufacture Patriot systems. However, during a Cabinet meeting at the presidential retreat at Camp David on Friday, Trump indicated that no final decision had yet been taken on the proposal.Meanwhile, a fire broke out at St Basil's Cathedral on Moscow's Red Square early Saturday before being brought under control, according to Russia's state-run TASS news agency.TASS, citing operational services, said the blaze started in the director's office on the first floor."On the first floor, in the director's office, personal belongings and furniture caught fire. The area of the fire was around 10 sq. metres," a source told the agency, as reported by Kyiv Post.The cause of the fire was not immediately known. No injuries were reported. Around 10 fire engines were deployed to the site before operational services confirmed that the fire had been extinguished, TASS said.
Article Summary: Russia launches barrage of ballistic missiles and drones targeting Ukraine's capital Kyiv. Attack damages residential buildings, sparks multiple fires and leaves people trapped under debris. Ukrainian president reiterates demand for additional Patriot air defence systems from the United States. Fire breaks out at Moscow's St Basil's Cathedral.

Article Title: Reeling from powerful earthquake that killed 34, Japan hit with 5.7 magnitude quake 5 days later
Article Text:
5.7-magnitude quake hits Northern Japan days after powerful tremor

This is a developing story

A 5.7-magnitude earthquake jolted Japan's northern Hokkaido region on Saturday, just days after a powerful 7.1 magnitude earthquake struck southwestern Japan.The 7.1-magnitude quake caused widespread destruction, triggering an explosion at a shopping mall, toppling a factory chimney and flattening homes in the city of Yatsushiro, while also leaving roads cracked and buildings damaged. The death toll from the quake rose to 34 by Friday.
Article Summary: A 5.7-magnitude earthquake jolted Japan's northern Hokkaido region on Saturday, just days after a powerful 7.1 magnitude earthquake struck southwestern Japan. The death toll from the quake rose to 34 by Friday.

Article Title: Broad Peak avalanche: Three of 10 missing climbers found dead in PoK
Article Text:
Broad Peak avalanche leaves three dead

Rescuers searching for 10 climbers missing after an avalanche on PoK's Broad Peak recovered three bodies on Friday after locating four victims, as harsh weather and poor flying conditions hampered helicopter search-and-rescue operations.The Gilgit-Baltistan regional government identified the three recovered bodies as Nepali climber Pur Bahadur Gurung, Omani climber Nathira Ahmed, and American climber Mallory Geis. Authorities said the bodies were transported to a hospital for further procedures, as cited by AP.Adverse weather continued to hamper rescue operations on Friday, with poor flying conditions limiting search efforts, Gilgit-Baltistan chief minister Amjad Hussain said in a statement.The announcement came hours after officials said search teams had located the bodies of four climbers, though the identity of the fourth victim has not yet been confirmed. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to brief the media.According to Karrar Haidri, vice president of the Alpine Club of Pakistan, the climbers lost contact with their base camp after an avalanche struck Broad Peak while they were attempting to scale the mountain.“The team has been out of communication since Thursday,” said Haidri, adding that Pakistan Army helicopters were assisting in the search-and-rescue operation.The expedition included five Nepali climbers, along with climbers from Oman, the United States, Pakistan, China, and another foreign national. The Pakistani climber was identified as Sohail Sakhi, while the Chinese climber was identified only by the surname Wang.China said it was working to verify whether any of its nationals were among the 10 climbers reported missing.The expedition was led by renowned mountaineer Nirmal Purja , a Nepal-born former British Army soldier widely known as Nims Dai. Purja gained global recognition after climbing the world's 14 highest peaks in a record 189 days in 2019, a feat documented in the Netflix film 14 Peaks: Nothing is Impossible. His record was later surpassed in 2023.Pakistan-based adventure company Moving Mountains said last month that the team had begun its journey to the town of Askole before attempting to summit Broad Peak, wishing the climbers a safe expedition.According to the company's website, the climb marked Mallory Geis' first attempt at an 8,000-metre peak in Pakistan. For Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi, a guide with the company, as well as a geographer and high-altitude photographer who had scaled several of the world's highest mountains, it was expected to be his final expedition to an 8,000-metre peak.Geis, 39, who lived in San Antonio, had announced on social media earlier this year that she was closing her Pilates studio to pursue mountaineering full time, writing that she was taking “a giant leap of faith into the unknown to see where life goes. I have a sneaking suspicion there will be lots of helmets, harnesses, and crampons involved.”At 8,047 metres (26,401 feet), Broad Peak is the world's 12th-highest mountain. It is located in PoK's Karakoram range, which is home to five of the world's 14 peaks above 8,000 metres and attracts mountaineers from across the globe.Mountaineering accidents are not uncommon in northern Pakistan, where climbers frequently contend with avalanches, harsh terrain and rapidly changing weather conditions.
Article Summary: Search teams have recovered the bodies of three of the 10 climbers missing after an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak. The bodies have been identified as Nepali climber Pur Bahadur Gurung, Omani climber Nathira Ahmed, and American climber Mallory Geis. The identity of the fourth victim has not been confirmed.

Article Title: US, Israel weigh bombarding Iran's energy infrastructure through the weekend: Report
Article Text:
US, Israel eye weekend bombing campaign on Iran's energy sites

The United States and Israel are planning a potential bombing campaign targeting Iran's energy infrastructure, with strikes possibly taking place over the weekend, CBS News reported on Friday, citing sources.However, US president Donald Trump has not yet given final approval for the operation.According to multiple US sources, officials have discussed wrapping up the operation before financial markets open on Monday amid concerns over the potential impact of the strikes on the US and global economy.However, no firm timeline has been finalised.The sources added that Israeli officials have been informed of the plans and are coordinating closely with the United States.A joint operation would mark Israel's return to active military operations after it paused its campaign during the US-brokered truce.Iran, meanwhile, has not launched attacks against Israel since the memorandum of understanding collapsed and the United States resumed combat operations in early July."Israel is unaware of a decision to restart full military operations, nor has been requested of Israel to join any military actions against Iran," an Israeli official was quoted as saying by CBS News.The development comes as Trump warned on Friday that Iran could be hit "very hard.""We'll be hitting him very hard and, you know, at some point they're going to say, 'We just can't take it anymore'," the US president said.The Wall Street Journal also reported that Trump had ordered preparations for a fresh military offensive aimed at pressuring Tehran into surrender, with the operation potentially beginning as early as this weekend.More than five months after the conflict began on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, the fighting shows no sign of easing, with both sides continuing to exchange attacks.Throughout the conflict, Trump has repeatedly threatened to target Iran's critical infrastructure. Last week, he warned that the United States would destroy a bridge or power plant each time commercial shipping in the strategically important Strait of Hormuz came under attack.The latest report also comes days after Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu met Trump and US defence secretary Pete Hegseth in Washington.
Article Summary: US, Israel eye weekend bombing campaign on Iran's energy sites, sources say. US president Donald Trump has not yet given final approval for the operation. Israeli officials have been informed of the plans and are coordinating closely with the United States. A joint operation would mark Israel's return to active military operations.

Article Title: ​From cancer survivors to surfing stars: California woman and her dog beat cancer before competing together at the World Dog Surfing Championships
Article Text:
Image credit: AP

From cancer survivors to world championship surfers

Rusty's surfing talent began as a puppy

Making waves at the World Dog Surfing Championships

What is the World Dog Surfing Championships?

More than a competition

A story that touched hearts

A California woman and her beloved Miniature Pinscher have become an inspiration after overcoming one of life's toughest challenges and returning to do what they love most together. Sophia Sadlowski, from Huntington Beach, California, and her dog Rusty, both survived cancer before competing side by side at the 2026 World Dog Surfing Championships held at Linda Mar Beach in Pacifica, California. Although they did not win the competition, their remarkable journey captured the hearts of spectators and highlighted the extraordinary bond between humans and their pets. Their appearance proved that resilience, determination and companionship can be just as memorable as standing on the winners' podium.Sophia Sadlowski and Rusty share a story that extends far beyond surfing. Both battled cancer and successfully recovered before returning to the sport they enjoy together. While Sadlowski has not publicly disclosed the specific types of cancer they faced, she confirmed that both she and Rusty are now cancer-free. Their participation at the championships served as a celebration of recovery and hope, inspiring fellow competitors and spectators alike.Rusty's surfing career started unexpectedly when Sadlowski placed him on a surfboard as a young puppy simply to take a photograph. Instead of jumping off, the Miniature Pinscher balanced himself with ease and rode a wave back to shore. Recognising his natural ability, Sadlowski continued training with him, and Rusty entered his first surfing competition at just four months old. He impressed judges by finishing third in his debut event, marking the beginning of an unusual sporting partnership.The duo competed together at the 10th World Dog Surfing Championships, held on August 1, 2026, at Linda Mar Beach in Pacifica, California. Rusty wore a green life jacket complete with a playful shark fin and protective dog goggles as he rode the waves alongside Sadlowski on the same surfboard. Their performance drew loud cheers from beachgoers, not only because of Rusty's surfing skills but also because of the inspiring journey that brought them to the event.The World Dog Surfing Championships were first held in 2016 and have since become one of the world's most unique canine sporting events. Dogs compete in categories based on their size, while additional tandem events allow multiple dogs or dogs and their owners to surf together. Judges assess competitors on factors including balance, confidence, ride duration, wave quality and overall style, rewarding dogs that demonstrate control and composure on the water.The annual event is designed to support animal welfare alongside competitive surfing. It raises funds for animal charities and rescue organisations while hosting pet adoption drives, educational activities and family-friendly entertainment. The championships encourage responsible pet ownership and celebrate the close relationship between people and their dogs, making the event about much more than trophies and rankings.Although Sophia Sadlowski and Rusty did not claim the championship title, they emerged as two of the event's most memorable participants. Their story reminded spectators that some victories cannot be measured by medals or podium finishes. After overcoming cancer together, simply standing on the same surfboard and sharing the waves represented a powerful triumph. Their journey from survivors to competitors continues to inspire people and demonstrates the resilience, trust and companionship that can exist between a person and their dog.
Article Summary: Sophia Sadlowski, from Huntington Beach, California, and her dog Rusty, both survived cancer before competing side by side at the 2026 World Dog Surfing Championships. Although they did not win the competition, their remarkable journey captured the hearts of spectators and highlighted the extraordinary bond between humans and their pets.

Article Title: 'Heartbreaking': Washington families return to burned homes as wildfires force mass evacuations

Raging wildfires consume dense timberlands in eastern Washington as a severe fire emergency forces mass evacuations across Spokane County.(Source: @theinformant_x)

What is the latest on the fires?

Pacific Northwest faces severe fire season

Residents returning to fire-hit communities in Spokane County, Washington, found homes destroyed after three fast-moving wildfires forced about 60,000 people to evacuate. Hundreds of structures were destroyed or damaged, and officials said it would take time to assess the full toll. No serious fire-related injuries or deaths had been reported.More than 600 structures had been damaged in the three fires, a toll that would put them among the most destructive in Washington’s history. Some residents returned to assess the damage and recover what belongings they could, while others waited to be allowed back into their neighbourhoods, CNN reported.Evacuees described leaving with little more than they could carry, and some stepped through hot rubble to retrieve possessions. One woman who lost her home of more than 21 years described the loss as “heartbreaking”, adding: “But we’re safe, so that’s all that matters.”The Autumn Lane Fire northwest of Spokane, which required the largest response on Sunday, remained “very active”, although crews had “relatively decent control” of its boundaries. It was the highest-priority fire in the US, while the other two blazes were holding.Crews were still trying to confirm that no one was missing or injured among the hundreds of destroyed structures.A fire chief said there remained a “potential for loss of life”. The cause of the three fires was under investigation.More than 10,000 residents remained without power, down from more than 30,000 at the peak. Officials said it would take time to allow affected residents to return safely to their neighbourhoods.Level 3 evacuation orders were issued for several areas, directing residents to leave immediately because of life-threatening conditions. A shelter opened at a local community college. Evacuations were also ordered at Spokane’s veterans’ hospital, water reclamation facility and waste-to-energy plant.Aircraft and bulldozers were among the resources deployed to fight 15 fires across Washington. More than 100 National Guard members were assisting the Spokane County community, while more than 4,000 personnel were battling fires across the state. Crews from more than a dozen states and Australia had also joined the response.Washington governor Bob Ferguson said he had spoken to US President Donald Trump, who was aware of the fires, and homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin. The state expected short-term assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to be approved and was working to request long-term aid.US senator Maria Cantwell said the Autumn Lane Fire’s designation as the country’s highest-priority blaze meant Washington would receive priority for federal resources. Ferguson had declared a statewide emergency and imposed a burn ban.Weather conditions improved after sustained winds of 20mph to 30mph, with gusts topping 40mph, swept through eastern Washington, including Spokane, for several hours on Saturday. By Sunday, winds had eased to between 5mph and 15mph, with gusts of up to 20mph.Fire weather concerns in eastern Washington fell from the highest Level 3 of 3 “extremely critical” category to a lower but still elevated Level 1 of 3 threat. Cooler temperatures were helping, but dry fuels, low humidity and occasional breezes meant existing fires and any new ones could still spread.Warmer and drier weather was expected to return to Spokane and eastern Washington by midweek. Winds from the north and northwest were forecast to carry smoke from regional wildfires, including fires in British Columbia, into parts of eastern Washington and northern Idaho. Air quality concerns could persist through the middle of the week.Washington was battling at least 10 large fires that had burned more than 425,000 acres this year, the most since 2021, amid a fourth consecutive year of drought.In Oregon, more than 1,300 wildfires had burned about 1.9 million acres this year. The Pacific Northwest was facing its worst fire season in more than 30 years.Nearly 30,000 fires had ignited across the US as of late spring, burning more than 2 million acres, the most in 14 years. Climate change had contributed to conditions favourable for wildfires and other disasters this summer.
Article Summary: More than 600 structures have been damaged in the three fires. The fires are among the most destructive in Washington's history. No serious fire-related injuries or deaths have been reported. More than 10,000 residents remained without power, down from more than 30,000.

Article Title: 'We'll see how it goes': Trump says Iran talks to begin Monday after halting planned strikes
Article Text:
Trump said diplomatic efforts involving Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Iran prompted him to call off what he described as a planned "massive attack"

US President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran will begin on Monday through intermediaries, signalling a renewed diplomatic push after he said he halted planned US military strikes following outreach by key Gulf nations.Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One, Trump said talks would begin on Monday afternoon and expressed hope for a negotiated settlement."We are talking to them in the form of a negotiation; it begins tomorrow afternoon, and we'll see how it goes. I'd rather make a deal. I'm not looking to kill people because a lot of people die," he said.Trump said diplomatic efforts involving Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Iran prompted him to call off what he described as a planned "massive attack" on Friday.He also said he expected an agreement on the Strait of Hormuz and expressed confidence that a deal could be reached on Iran's denuclearisation.The diplomatic push comes as regional mediators work to revive an understanding between Washington and Tehran. Israeli media reported that intermediaries are trying to restore a memorandum of understanding signed last month to keep the Strait of Hormuz open and free of transit fees for 60 days.Iranian state media also reported that talks between Iran and Oman on a joint mechanism to manage the strategic waterway were in their final stages.The earlier framework reportedly broke down over differing interpretations. Trump maintained the strait would remain permanently open, while Tehran said the arrangement preserved Iran's sovereign control over the shipping route.According to reports, Qatari officials held intensive discussions with Iran, the US and Oman over the weekend before informing Trump that Tehran had accepted a proposal related to the strait. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman also spoke to Trump, urging restraint.Trump later announced on Truth Social that he was pausing the planned strikes, citing progress in talks on the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's nuclear programme.However, Iranian military officials rejected Trump's account, calling it false. A source linked to Iran's delegation also told the semi-official Fars News Agency that no formal agreement on the Strait of Hormuz had yet been reached.The Wall Street Journal reported that Gulf allies remain divided on Iran, with Saudi Arabia advocating restraint while the United Arab Emirates has urged Washington to take stronger military action against Tehran.
Article Summary: Trump said diplomatic efforts involving Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Iran prompted him to call off what he described as a planned "massive attack" He also said he expected an agreement on the Strait of Hormuz and expressed confidence that a deal could be reached on Iran's denuclearisation.

Article Title: Locked, loaded ... and put on hold: Another bewildering Trump pivot on Iran
Article Text:
Donald Trump says he is holding off US strikes on Iran as negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz continue.

TOI correspondent from Washington: US President Donald Trump on Sunday announced yet again that he was calling off a threatened American military strike on Iran for now in the diplomatic equivalent of hitting the brakes on sighting a speed camera on the highway.After warning that the United States was "locked and loaded" with military power "not seen since World War II," Trump declared on Truth Social that he is canceling the attack because Iran and several Middle Eastern countries had requested time to finalize what he described as the "parameters of a deal."The proposed understanding, according to the President, would include the immediate reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to Iran's nuclear threat. "Get to work, everybody, and get it DONE," Trump exhorted, capping another dizzying turn in a presidency where foreign policy increasingly resembles a roller coaster designed by a rogue algorithm.For diplomats, allies and military planners, the latest pivot was less surprising than the speed with which it arrived. Over the past several months, Washington's Iran policy has swung between promises of overwhelming force and optimistic declarations that peace is just one phone call and one negotiated paragraph away.Markets, insurers and airlines have found themselves reading presidential social media posts almost as closely as intelligence assessments.Behind the scenes, however, serious diplomacy appears to be afoot. Qatar and other Gulf mediators have reportedly shuttled proposals between Washington and Tehran aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with Saudi Crown Prince MBS also urging dialogue while seeking greater clarity on Washington's long-term strategy. Whether that strategy exists in a form recognizable to anyone outside the Oval Office remains an open question.Teheran, for all the battering it is taking, wasted little time taunting Trump's announcement as a retreat, with Mohammad Marandi, an Iranian gadabout, warning that if Trump proceeds with his threat, there will be no turning back for Iran, “which will respond decisively and strike with full force.”Meanwhile, US military realities have complicated the political messaging with reports of growing pressure on American military resources after months of sustained operations in the region. US defense officials have acknowledged the strain imposed by repeated deployments of missile-defense assets, although the Pentagon continues to insist that its forces remain capable of meeting operational requirements. Analysts note that balancing commitments across the Middle East, Europe and the Indo-Pacific has become an increasingly delicate exercise.The political battlefield at home is starting to become even more challenging as Trump's approval ratings have slipped amid mounting domestic controversies and growing voter fatigue over multiple simultaneous crises. Particularly striking has been the revolt within parts of his own America First coalition, where conservative commentator Tucker Carlson, former lawmaker Marjorie Taylor Greene, Congressman Thomas Massie and former counterterrorism official Joe Kent have all voiced sharp criticism of renewed military involvement overseas.Weekend reports of a meeting among several of those figures fueled speculation about a possible new political movement dedicated to restoring what they argue was the original anti-interventionist promise of the MAGA agenda. Whether such discussions evolve into an actual political party remains uncertain, but the symbolism alone underscores widening fractures on the American right.Trump has spent recent days lashing out at opponents over a succession of controversies, including criticism surrounding the nomination of his former personal lawyer Todd Blanche as AG. Over the weekend, amid melting down at his own prosecutors who withdrew a case against a former Olympian falsely accused of causing damage to the Lincoln memorial reflecting pool, Trump was busy posting AI slop with the enthusiasm of a high-school sophomore, broadening his already expansive catalogue of political grievances and historical fantasy. The familiar formula – counterattack, escalate, denounce, pivot and declare victory with AI slop – has become almost ritualistic.For American voters and the country's allies, the challenge is no longer deciphering Trump's latest posts but determining whether it will still represent US policy by breakfast.
Article Summary: Donald Trump says he is holding off US strikes on Iran as negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz continue. Qatar and other Gulf mediators have reportedly shuttled proposals between Washington and Tehran aimed at reopening the Strait. The familiar formula – counterattack, escalate, denounce, pivot and declare victory with AI slop – has become almost ritualistic.

Article Title: An Arizona baby stopped breathing during a post-office visit; former nurse Mary Schwarz performed CPR and helped restore her breathing on the way to hospital
Article Text:
An 8-month-old baby, Nova, is recovering in a Tucson hospital after a postal worker performed CPR and saved her life.Photo credit: Fox10

A nurse’s instinct kicked in

Police arrived within moments

A frightening moment for a mother

Nova’s health battle didn’t start there

Why CPR training matters

A community connection

A routine errand, a life saved

What started as an ordinary stop at a post office in Clifton, Arizona, turned into a life-or-death emergency when an 8-month-old baby stopped breathing. Thanks to the fast response of a former nurse working behind the counter, the child survived long enough to reach medical care.The baby’s mother, Kylie Vega, had brought her daughter Nova to the Greenlee County post office on July 11 to mail a package. Within moments, Vega realised something was seriously wrong. Nova went limp, and Vega said she began patting the baby’s back after noticing she was no longer breathing, as per reports.Help came from an unexpected place: the postal clerk at the counter. Mary Schwarz, who had worked as a nurse for 13 years before becoming a postal clerk, immediately stepped in when she saw the baby in distress. Schwarz said there was no hesitation; she simply acted.After checking for a pulse and finding none, Schwarz began CPR. When she heard Vega tell the 911 dispatcher that the baby may have tried to vomit and could be choking, she also performed back thrusts to try to clear Nova’s airway.That combination of CPR and airway-clearing efforts was crucial in the first few minutes of the emergency, when every second mattered.Clifton Police Lt. Shari Aguilar happened to be nearby and responded quickly. She already knew Schwarz had a nursing background, and she immediately joined in to help stabilise the infant.Aguilar then made the decision to get Nova to a nearby clinic as fast as possible rather than wait for an ambulance. Schwarz held the baby in the front passenger seat while Aguilar drove.Nova reportedly began breathing again about halfway to the clinic, before medical staff took over. She was later transferred to Banner University Medical Center in Tucson for additional treatment.For Vega, the scene was terrifying. She had gone to the post office for something routine, then suddenly found herself watching her baby struggle to breathe. Afterward, she said she was deeply grateful for the people who stepped in so quickly.She praised Schwarz for saving her daughter’s life and said she is thankful that there are still kind people in the world willing to act in an emergency. Vega also described Nova as “the rainbow” in her life, saying the baby is especially precious after everything she has already been through.This frightening episode was not Nova’s first medical challenge. Vega said the baby was born with a hole in her heart and without one of the arteries needed to support it. Nova underwent surgery on July 21 to repair the hole, and she remains hospitalised as she recovers, according to Fox 10.That background makes the post office rescue even more remarkable. Nova had already faced serious health issues at just 8 months old, and the timely response from Schwarz and Aguilar helped get her to care when she needed it most.Schwarz said the experience is a powerful reminder of how important CPR training can be. She noted that emergencies do not just happen in hospitals or on the roadside; they can happen at home, at a pool, or in an everyday place like a post office.Her point is a simple one: knowing what to do before an emergency happens can save a life. In this case, that training made the difference between panic and a rapid, effective response.The story did not end when Nova reached the hospital. Vega said she and Schwarz have since become Facebook friends, and she continues to keep the former nurse updated on her daughter’s recovery.That ongoing connection gives the rescue a human ending that goes beyond the emergency itself. It is now a story not only about survival, but also about gratitude, community and the kind of split-second action that can change a family forever.It is the kind of incident that reminds people how quickly life can change. One minute, Vega was mailing a package. The next, she was relying on a stranger’s medical instincts and a police officer’s fast decision-making to help save her baby’s life.Thanks to Mary Schwarz’s calm response, Lt. Aguilar’s urgency and Vega’s quick call for help, Nova made it to the clinic breathing again. For her family, that is a result they will never forget.
Article Summary: An 8-month-old baby stopped breathing at a post office in Clifton, Arizona. Postal clerk Mary Schwarz, who had worked as a nurse for 13 years before becoming a postal clerk, performed CPR and airway-clearing efforts. A police officer happened to be nearby and joined in to help stabilise the infant. Nova began breathing again about halfway to the clinic, before medical staff took over. She was later transferred to Banner University Medical Center in Tucson.

Article Title: New Orleans collected 9,000 discarded Christmas trees and airlifted them into coastal wetlands; the programme has restored marsh equal to nearly 200 football fields
Article Text:
A helicopter dropping its first bundle of trees for the Christmas tree drop restoration project (US fish and wild life service photos)

Louisiana loses coastal land

Christmas trees come to rescue

Staff from Bayou Sauvage National Wildlife Refuge drive an airboat to where the Christmas trees are dropped

Trees help rebuild marshes

Research supports method

How much land has been restored?

Every year after Christmas, thousands of used trees are thrown away. In New Orleans, however, many of them get a second use. Instead of ending up in landfill, the trees are collected, tied into large bundles and dropped by helicopters into coastal marshes to help slow land loss.The programme has been running for nearly 30 years and is part of a effort to protect Louisiana's disappearing coastline, according to Ecotias. The recycled trees are placed in shallow wetlands, where they help trap mud and reduce the force of moving water. Over time, this gives marsh plants a better chance to grow and helps strengthen the wetlands.Scientists say this has helped create and stabilise hundreds of acres of marshland and has become an example of how waste materials can support environmental restoration.Louisiana has lost nearly 2,000 square miles, or more than 5,000 square kilometres, of coastal land since the 1930s. The loss has happened because of several reasons.Coastlines naturally wear away through erosion. Powerful storms can remove large amounts of land in a short time. Rising sea levels add more pressure, while the ground itself is slowly sinking in a natural process known as subsidence.Another major reason is that the Mississippi River no longer deposits as much sediment into nearby wetlands as it once did.Sediment refers to small particles of soil, sand and mud carried by water. In the past, floods spread this material across marshes, helping replace land that had been lost. Today, changes to the river have reduced that natural process.As a result, many wetlands are disappearing faster than they can recover. These marshes help absorb floodwater, reduce the impact of waves and provide a home for many plants and animals. They also help protect nearby roads, railway lines and communities during storms, although experts say they cannot fully protect against hurricanes.One of the areas receiving attention is Bayou Sauvage Urban National Wildlife Refuge, located next to New Orleans East. It contains some of the last remaining marshland between Lakes Pontchartrain and Borgne.After the holiday season, residents are asked to donate their natural Christmas trees instead of throwing them away. Only real trees are accepted. Before collection, people must remove all decorations, including lights, ornaments, tinsel, artificial snow, tree stands and other materials. This ensures that only natural wood enters the wetlands.The City of New Orleans works with its sanitation and resilience teams, the US Fish and Wildlife Service and the Louisiana Army National Guard to carry out the project.In March 2025, nearly 9,000 Christmas trees were collected. Workers tied them into bundles before helicopters lifted them to selected areas inside the wildlife refuge.After the trees were dropped, crews travelling by boat adjusted their positions where needed. The helicopter flights also served as training exercises for National Guard pilots and crew members.According to refuge officials, each bundle usually contains around 50 to 60 trees. A helicopter can carry three or four bundles at a time using special lifting equipment. The bundles are placed in straight lines at locations selected in advance. Once the trees are released, crews recover the reusable lifting gear.The bundles of trees act like permeable barriers. This means water can still flow through them, but more slowly. As the water loses speed, it drops the sediment it is carrying instead of washing it away.Over time, more mud and silt collect around the branches. As these materials build up, the ground slowly becomes higher and more stable.This creates better conditions for marsh grasses to grow. Once established, the grasses help hold the soil together with their roots and make the marsh stronger. The restored areas also provide habitat for birds, fish, crabs, crawfish and shrimp.Pon Dixson, a project leader at the refuge, explais, "The trees are doing what they're designed to do."The trees themselves are not expected to last forever. Instead, they act as temporary support while sediment and plant roots gradually create a stronger and more permanent marsh ridge. That ridge can then reduce everyday wave action and erosion.Scientists have studied this approach for many years. A field study published in Ecological Engineering in 1997 examined recycled Christmas-tree fences at two marsh sites in Louisiana.The study found that the tree barriers reduced wave energy reaching the marsh bed by about half in the test areas. Researchers also found that sediment built up at rates of up to about 1.3 inches each year in some sheltered locations. At one monitoring site, vegetation returned after around three years. However, other locations remained without plant growth.Scientists say the success of the method depends greatly on where the barriers are placed. If the water is too deep, sediment may still collect, but it could take many years before the land becomes shallow enough for marsh plants to grow.The researchers also stressed that Christmas-tree barriers cannot stop the wider processes causing Louisiana's land loss. Instead, they work best as part of larger restoration efforts.The exact amount of land restored is not completely clear because official estimates have varied over time. By 2023, federal refuge managers reported that the annual Christmas tree programme had created 115 acres.Later updates from the city described the restored area using football field comparisons. One announcement referred to about 200 football fields, while another in March 2025 mentioned around 330 football fields. A later update returned to roughly 200 football fields.The programme continued during the 2025-26 holiday season. In July 2026, Louisiana National Guard crews also delivered donated Christmas trees to another vulnerable marsh near Madisonville on the north shore of Lake Pontchartrain.
Article Summary: New Orleans residents are asked to donate their natural Christmas trees instead of throwing them away. The recycled trees are placed in shallow wetlands, where they help trap mud and reduce the force of moving water. Scientists say this has helped create and stabilise hundreds of acres of marshland and has become an example of how waste materials can support environmental restoration.

Article Title: US general warns Pentagon he lacks naval assets to keep shielding Israel from missiles: Report
Article Text:
General Alexus Grynkewich. (AP photo)

Military assets under pressure

Iran conflict adds to strain

Stockpile concerns grow

The top US military commander overseeing operations in Europe has reportedly warned the Pentagon that American forces may soon be unable to sustain missile-defence operations for Israel without additional naval assets, The Washington Post reported.According to The Washington Post, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, commander of the US European Command (EUCOM), wrote to senior Pentagon officials this week that he could be forced to prioritise defending the US homeland over Israel if another US Navy destroyer is not placed under his command.Grynkewich's warning came amid rising pressure on US military resources after months of operations linked to the conflict involving Iran.EUCOM oversees US military operations in Europe and the Mediterranean, where American destroyers have helped intercept ballistic missiles fired at Israel from Iran as well as attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.According to the report, the US currently has five destroyers based in Rota, Spain, available for deployment to the eastern Mediterranean, with a sixth expected to join the fleet later this year.As of Friday, two destroyers were operating in the Mediterranean while three remained at the Spanish naval base.The prolonged deployment has reportedly increased wear on the vessels while also consuming advanced interceptor missiles, raising concerns within the Pentagon about the sustainability of current operations.Following the collapse of the US-Iran ceasefire in early July, the US has maintained a significant naval presence closer to Iran.Multiple warships, including aircraft carriers and at least 11 destroyers, have been deployed to support operations in the region and safeguard shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.The newspaper noted that EUCOM's responsibilities also include protecting NATO allies against potential Russian threats, including long-range missile risks, adding to the pressure on available military resources.The reported warning comes amid broader concerns over US interceptor missile stockpiles.Earlier reports have indicated that months of defending Israel against missile attacks have significantly reduced American inventories of advanced missile-defence interceptors, prompting worries about sustaining future operations.
Article Summary: Gen. Alexus Grynkewich wrote to senior Pentagon officials this week. Warned he could be forced to prioritise defending the US homeland over Israel. Comes amid rising pressure on US military resources after months of operations linked to the conflict involving Iran.

Article Title: Researchers mapped 128 million US buildings for landslide exposure; 6.5 million Americans live in danger zones concentrated across Appalachia and the West Coast
Article Text:
Landslides cause about 25 deaths a year in the USA

Mapping local risk at the building level

Population density increases eastern exposure

The urban-rural recovery gap

Different policy solutions for cities and rural areas

Why better mapping matters

An estimated 6.5 million Americans live in homes built on or next to landslide-prone land, according to a major national study by the University of Washington.By studying 128 million buildings across the United States, researchers created the Landslide Exposure Database (LED). It is the first detailed national map showing how landslide hazards overlap with where people live.The findings, published in Earth's Future, an AGU journal focused on sustainability, reveal a major gap between urban and rural communities in both landslide risk and their ability to recover.Unlike large disasters such as hurricanes or floods, landslides affect very small areas where the level of danger can change sharply over short distances."The susceptibility at one location can be vastly different than the susceptibility at a neighboring location just 10, 20 or 30 meters away," said Joseph Wartman, a civil engineer at the University of Washington and co-author of the study. "We have never considered the human geography of landslides; this is really the first attempt to do that."To create this detailed map, lead author Daniel Acosta-Reyes and his team combined USGS landslide maps, building footprint data, and nighttime occupancy models.Nighttime occupancy helps estimate risk when people are asleep and less able to evacuate quickly."This is really a template that we should be able to duplicate in other nations and other parts of the world," Acosta-Reyes said.Although the steepest mountains are in the western US, Alaska, and Hawaii, these regions have fewer people, so they account for only a small share of those exposed to landslides. Together, the Rocky Mountains, Alaska, and Hawaii make up about 4% of the exposed population.Instead, more than half of Americans living in landslide-prone areas are in eastern states. Because of higher population density, even relatively flat states such as Illinois, Minnesota, and Nebraska have more than 700,000 people living on or near hazardous slopes.The researchers also used US Census Bureau socio-economic data to study how well communities can recover after landslides.
