Rural residents make up 62% of people living in landslide-prone areas, but they often have fewer financial resources and less public infrastructure to rebuild after damage."Technically, a landslide is not insurable, so if you lose your home in a minor landslide event, that's going to be a personal expense and a catastrophic loss for the homeowner," said Ben Mirus, a USGS research geologist who was not involved in the study.This problem is especially clear in the Appalachian Highlands, from northern Maine to central Alabama. In West Virginia, where 70% of the state is prone to landslides, the high cost of rare flat land pushes many lower-income families to live on steep, more dangerous hillsides."We have found that this urban-rural divide plays out across the entire United States," Wartman said. He added that wealthier cities often reduce risk by building high-density housing on flat land or by using engineering to make hillside developments safer.For wealthier cities where people choose to build homes on scenic but risky slopes, such as Seattle and San Francisco, the researchers recommend stricter zoning rules and policies that place recovery costs on homeowners.For lower-income rural areas, especially in Appalachia where housing choices are limited, the study recommends more public investment in early warning systems, rainfall monitoring, and federal disaster assistance.Researchers say the new database could help governments make better decisions long before a landslide happens. Instead of relying only on broad regional hazard maps, officials can now identify individual buildings and neighborhoods that may face higher risk. This allows local authorities to prioritise inspections, improve evacuation planning, and target investments in protective infrastructure where they are needed most. The same approach could also help emergency managers estimate how many people might be affected during heavy rainfall or other triggering events.The database is also expected to support future research into how changing weather patterns may influence landslide exposure. Scientists have long recognised that intense rainfall is one of the biggest triggers for landslides in many parts of the United States. As climate change increases the frequency of extreme precipitation in several regions, communities already located on unstable slopes could face greater risks over time, making accurate exposure mapping even more valuable for long-term planning. While the database does not predict when or where the next landslide will occur, it provides a stronger foundation for land-use planning, disaster preparedness, and public awareness by showing where people and infrastructure are most exposed.
Article Summary: Landslide Exposure Database is the first detailed national map showing how landslide hazards overlap with where people live. Findings reveal a major gap between urban and rural communities in both landslide risk and their ability to recover. Researchers say the new database could help governments make better decisions long before a landslide happens.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jim Brown: "I set my standards so high, no one could be harsher on me than…" - a simple philosophy behind extraordinary success and discipline
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jim Brown (Image: Wikipedia)

Quote of the day by Jim Brown

"I set my standards so high, no one could be harsher on me than I was"

Understand the meaning behind Jim Brown’s quote

Where this quote actually comes from

Why personal standards matter more than public opinion

Why real accountability starts with yourself first

Why discipline produces consistency that motivation alone cannot

Why the goal was never actually perfection

Why criticism gets easier to handle once real standards exist

Why this idea clearly reaches beyond sport entirely

A note on Jim Brown's legacy

Other famous quotes by Jim Brown

"There were a lot of running backs as good as me. The real difference was that I could focus. I never laid back and relied on natural ability."

"The power is between your ears. The power is in your heart."

"I don't teach kids to be number 1. What I teach is to be as good as you can be. Use what you have and be as good as you can be. That's all you can do, anyway."

"You can't get old without living."

Why this quote is relevant

Success often gets credited to talent, opportunity or simple luck. Jim Brown , widely regarded as one of the greatest American football players in history, pointed somewhere else entirely. "I set my standards so high, no one could be harsher on me than I was," he said. His toughest critic was never an opposing team or someone in the media. It was his own expectation of himself, set high enough that outside judgment genuinely could not compete with it, a discipline that carried him through nine remarkable seasons in the NFL and continued shaping how he lived the rest of his life afterwards.Brown is describing where his real accountability actually came from. He was not relying on coaches, critics or public opinion to push him harder than he already pushed himself. He had already set personal standards demanding enough that no outside judgement could realistically exceed them. This reflects genuine self-discipline, not self-punishment. It encourages people to chase real improvement by focusing on their own growth rather than constantly seeking approval from someone else.This line is documented in Out of Bounds, Brown's 1990 memoir written with Steve Delsohn, published by Kensington Publishing Corporation. Brown has also spoken directly about what actually separated him from other talented runners of his era. "There were a lot of running backs as good as me," he said. "The real difference was that I could focus. I never laid back and relied on natural ability." That is really the same idea from today's quote, stated from a slightly different angle.People often spend a huge amount of energy worrying about what other people think of them. Feedback genuinely has value, but relying entirely on outside validation tends to limit someone rather than help them. People with strong personal standards evaluate their own work honestly, regardless of whether praise or criticism happens to be coming their way at the time. Their motivation comes from actually doing their best, not from impressing anyone watching.Blaming circumstances is always the easier option when something goes wrong. People who genuinely succeed over the long run tend to ask a different question instead, what could I have actually done better here. Taking that kind of responsibility does not mean expecting perfection from yourself. It means recognising that real improvement starts with honest self-reflection, focused specifically on whatever you can actually control.Motivation rises and falls depending on the day. Discipline stays in place regardless. High personal standards keep effort consistent even once the initial enthusiasm has faded. Brown became one of the greatest players in the sport not purely through natural ability, but because he approached his own preparation with real, sustained commitment, exactly the trait he describes in his own words above.None of this should be read as demanding literal perfection. Nobody performs flawlessly every single time, and Brown himself never claimed otherwise. What his quote really reflects is a commitment to continuous improvement, using high standards to encourage genuine growth rather than fear. The actual goal was becoming better than yesterday, not becoming flawless overnight.People with strong internal standards tend to be less shaken by outside criticism. Constructive feedback starts to function as useful information rather than a personal attack, since they have already examined their own performance honestly before anyone else even weighs in. Confidence tends to grow once self-evaluation actually matters more than public judgement.Brown's underlying philosophy applies just as well outside football. Students working toward academic excellence, entrepreneurs building a business from scratch, scientists chasing a genuine discovery, artists refining their own craft. In every field, long-term success tends to depend less on outside pressure and more on a genuine personal commitment to keep improving.Jim Brown, who lived from 1936 to 2023, is widely regarded as one of the greatest running backs in the history of American football. Across nine seasons with the Cleveland Browns, he led the league in rushing multiple times and was named the NFL's Most Valuable Player on several occasions. He retired from football at the peak of his career to pursue acting, and later devoted much of his life to community programmes and social advocacy.Brown's words are a reminder that real excellence rarely comes from fear of criticism. It grows out of the discipline to hold yourself accountable even when nobody else is actually watching. People who genuinely maintain high personal standards keep learning and improving regardless of whether outside recognition ever arrives at all. The standards someone chooses for themselves, far more than the world's judgement of their achievements, are usually what end up shaping their actual character and the legacy they eventually leave behind.
Article Summary: Jim Brown is widely regarded as one of the greatest American football players in history. His quote of the day reflects a commitment to continuous improvement. It encourages people to chase real improvement by focusing on their own growth rather than constantly seeking approval from someone else. Students working toward academic excellence, entrepreneurs and artists refining their own craft all benefit from Brown's philosophy.

Article Title: Family to sue US government after Haitian woman froze to death following ICE release: Report
Article Text:
Haitian woman who froze to death after ICE release. (AP Photo)

Released after months in custody

Attorney alleges 'very bad judgment call'

Death ruled homicide

DHS rejects responsibility

Family says they never got promised call

The family of a 31-year-old Haitian immigrant who froze to death after being released by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Pittsburgh is preparing to sue the federal government and multiple other entities, according to a report by The Guardian.The report said the lawsuit is expected to be filed within the next two to three weeks. The family alleges that authorities released Daphy Michel, who was suffering from severe mental illness, without ensuring she could safely return home.Michel was later found dead at a bus shelter, and Pennsylvania officials ruled her death a homicide caused by hypothermia.Michel had spent six months in a Pennsylvania county jail after a reported mental health crisis and a street incident. After a judge dismissed the charges against her in late February, ICE took her into custody before releasing her in south Pittsburgh with an ankle monitor.According to The Guardian, she was expected to return to Charleroi, around 20 miles (32 km) away, but never made it home. Surveillance footage reportedly showed her remaining at a bus shelter for nearly 24 hours.She was wearing summer clothes despite temperatures dropping to about 20°F (-6.6°C).She was later taken to hospital, where she died.Joseph Murphy, an attorney representing Michel's family, told The Guardian that the lawsuit would target the United States along with "multiple other governmental and non-governmental entities.""Anybody who knew Daphy for more than one minute knew there was something wrong with her. It was a real dumb thing to just release her like that in February in Pittsburgh... It was a very bad judgment call," Murphy said.He argued that Michel's mental illness was obvious, that she did not speak English, and that her phone was effectively unusable because its service plan had expired while she was in jail.In June, the Allegheny County Medical Examiner's Office ruled Michel's death a homicide, stating she was a vulnerable adult suffering from untreated severe mental illness and a significant language barrier when she was released from federal custody.Officials clarified that the homicide ruling does not assign criminal liability but indicates that another person's actions contributed to the death. Pittsburgh police are investigating the case.The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE's parent agency, has previously denied responsibility for Michel's death.According to The Guardian, DHS said in an earlier statement that Michel died three days after being released, adding that she had been released with all her belongings, including a fully charged phone, in sunny weather where public transportation was available. The agency also described her as being in the US illegally.Murphy disputed those claims, saying Michel had entered the US legally, had been granted humanitarian status, and had an asylum application pending. He also said her mobile phone service had lapsed during her incarceration.Michel's brother said the family had expected to collect her after her release from jail and had been told they would receive a call when she was freed. Instead, the next call they received came from a Pittsburgh hospital informing them that she had died.Advocates told The Guardian that Michel's case reflects broader concerns about how vulnerable immigrants with mental health issues are released from detention without adequate support or transport to their destinations. They said similar practices have been observed under previous administrations as well.
Article Summary: Daphy Michel, 31, died after being released by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Pittsburgh. Family says they never got promised call when she was freed. Lawsuit is expected to be filed within the next two to three weeks. ICE has denied responsibility for Michel's death.

Article Title: In 2022, a Wisconsin retirement community began housing college students; they now pay about $500 monthly and volunteer eight hours each week with older residents
Article Text:
The programme is designed for students who genuinely want to engage with older residents rather than simply save money. (Picture credit: Marquette)

Volunteering for low rent

A growing trend

Shared living helps reduce loneliness among both students and older adults. (Picture: Catholic Herald)

Beating loneliness together

Building genuine bonds

Indian student finds family

For 23-year-old Indian student Shojin Samson, moving to the United States did not mean living in a student hostel or sharing an apartment. Instead, he found himself surrounded by hundreds of older neighbours, a decision that helped him save on rent while finding the family connection he had long missed.When most students move to university, they look for housemates their own age. But Some students in the United States are doing the opposite. Instead of noisy student flats and late-night parties, some college students are ending their evenings in quiet retirement communities. In return for affordable rent, they volunteer a few hours each week and build friendships with older residents.For students, the arrangement provides a safe place to live, lower living costs and a sense of community. For older residents, it brings regular company, fresh energy and meaningful interactions. Programmes like these are slowly expanding in the United States as organisations look for ways to address both housing affordability and loneliness.One such student is 25-year-old Daija Holliday, who moved from North Carolina to attend Marquette University in Milwaukee. Instead of renting a regular apartment, she chose to live at St Camillus Life Plan Community, a retirement community with more than 600 older residents.Holliday says she grew up in her grandparents' home, so living among older adults felt natural to her. She believes the experience has given her much more than an affordable place to stay. "It's my family away from home. I always feel like they have my back," she says, as quoted by Market Watch.Holliday pays about $500 a month for an independent apartment at St Camillus. According to the programme, that is around one-third of the local market rent for a one-bedroom apartment. In return, she volunteers for eight hours every week while studying counselling psychology at Marquette University.Her volunteer work includes sharing coffee and newspapers with residents, helping them with errands, leading Saturday morning fitness classes and organising game nights.The programme offers a different lifestyle from a traditional student residence, where evenings are often busy with social events.According to her, the arrangement works well for her, although it may not suit everyone. "By 7.30 or 8, things get pretty quiet here. If you're looking for more activity at night, this is not for you," Holliday said.According to Sheri Steinig, director of strategic initiatives and communications at the nonprofit Generations United, Holliday is among a growing number of young adults living with older people in different settings. Some live in retirement communities, while others take part in home-sharing arrangements where students and seniors share living space.Steinig says the idea helps address two challenges at the same time- rising housing costs and increasing loneliness. "People get out of their silos and live the way people used to live, which was more intergenerationally," she says."When people are living together, there's the opportunity for spontaneous interaction, rather than formal events. There's immediacy to connecting when people are in the same space," Steinig adds.Similar programmes have started elsewhere. Last year, St Olaf College in Minnesota introduced an initiative that allows students to live in retirement-community townhouses while interacting with older residents.The Marquette programme itself began in 2022. It was inspired by an intergenerational living programme launched in the Netherlands in 2012. Under that model, university students live rent-free in small apartments inside the Humanitas retirement community in exchange for spending at least 30 hours every month with older residents.In 2023, former US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy described loneliness as a public health epidemic. He said loneliness carries health risks similar to smoking 15 cigarettes a day and is linked to higher risks of cardiovascular disease, dementia, stroke, depression, anxiety and premature death.Older adults often face social isolation because of reduced mobility, limited transport options or the loss of family members and caregivers. At the same time, many younger people also experience loneliness after moving away from home for studies or work. These programmes thus help tackle loneliness, stereotypes and age-related prejudice, across generations.Jennifer Molinsky, director of the Housing an Aging Society Programme at the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies, says these living arrangements benefit both age groups. "There's vital intergenerational connections to be made. It's an opportunity to connect across generations. A chance to broaden everyone's horizons," she says."Loneliness is an epidemic among both young people and older people. Living together helps bring different energy, skills and opportunities into the space that we wouldn't normally have. It helps counter stereotypes," she adds.The Marquette programme is led by Stacy Barnes, director of the Wisconsin Geriatric Education Center. She says the programme is open to students from all academic backgrounds and age groups. However, those who have joined so far have mainly been graduate students or those pursuing higher-level studies.Five students are expected to live at St. Camillus this autumn. Students who join are expected to enjoy spending time with older adults rather than simply looking for low-cost housing.Barnes says the programme is designed for students who genuinely want to engage with older residents rather than simply save money. "We're interested in students who are looking for more than cheap rent," Barnes says."We're looking for a level of maturity. Someone who is motivated to live with 600-plus older adults and open to genuine social interactions and sees the potential value in connecting with older adults," Barnes adds.Students also have access to facilities within the retirement community, including a gym, swimming pool, movie theatre, restaurants, lounges and a pub. To encourage interaction, St Camillus also gives each student a monthly dining credit to use at the community's restaurants so they can share meals with residents.Among the students living at St Camillus is 23-year-old Shojin Samson, who moved from India to study at Marquette University. Coming to the United States was his first experience of living abroad and his first introduction to American culture.Samson says the retirement community felt familiar because it reminded him of the mixed-age communities he knew back home. He also found it easy to build friendships with the older residents.For Samson, the experience became deeply personal because he lost his grandparents when he was around six years old. "I have always had this void. There's this space I'd like to fill in my life. I'm very delighted and blessed and thrilled to say I have got so many grandparents now," he says.Jeremy Pust, executive director of independent living at St Camillus, says the presence of younger people has also had a positive effect on residents."The younger generation provides a sense of youth, comfort and companionship, especially for some residents who don't have family or who have family living far away. It's pretty magical when you see the connections happen," he says.
Article Summary: Shared living helps reduce loneliness among both students and older adults. Some college students are ending their evenings in quiet retirement communities. For students, the arrangement provides a safe place to live, lower living costs and a sense of community. For older residents, it brings regular company, fresh energy and meaningful interactions.

Article Title: Pakistan restricts digital news websites reporting on PoK protests, crackdowns: Report
Article Text:
Pakistan expands online curbs following coverage of PoK unrest

Pakistan has reportedly expanded digital censorship measures by restricting access to several news websites following extensive media coverage of the ongoing unrest in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK).Alongside the reported blocking of local and regional news websites, international broadcasters, have also become inaccessible to users in parts of Pakistan, according to media reports cited by ANI.The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK). Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions.The channels facing possible blocking include those linked to Pakistan's main opposition party, its leader and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, as well as several journalists critical of the government, according to a court order dated June 24.Earlier in July, Al Jazeera reported that a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad had ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels based on a June 2 report by Pakistan's National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA).The agency alleged that the channels had published content that was "intimidating", "provocative" and "derogatory" towards state institutions and public officials.Al Jazeera reported that digital rights groups have warned the proposed bans could further restrict freedom of expression in Pakistan. With television and print media facing significant curbs, social media remains one of the few platforms for public debate and dissent, the report said.The broadcaster also reported that YouTube had notified 27 content creators that their channels could be blocked if they failed to comply with the court's directives.The restrictions come amid heightened sensitivity over the flow of information related to the political situation and local protests in PoK.The second phase of elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) was marred by widespread disruptions, logistical challenges and continuing protests, raising fresh concerns over the credibility of the electoral process.Polling was held across 21 constituencies, including nine in the Muzaffarabad Division of PoK and 12 refugee constituencies located in different parts of Pakistan.Voting was disrupted in several constituencies as road blockades and protests affected access to polling stations and delayed the electoral process.
Article Summary: Pakistani authorities have not officially confirmed the reported restrictions. The restrictions appear to target platforms covering the recent protests, alleged security crackdowns and growing public discontent in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) Earlier in July, a judicial magistrate's court in Islamabad ordered the blocking of several YouTube channels.

Article Title: 'Double tap': How terrorists are trapping Pakistan's security personnel
Article Text:
The latest assault came on Sunday, when a suicide bomber struck outside a police station in Swat's Kabal town during an anti-terror rally

A 'double tap' strategy to maximise casualties

Recent attacks expose worsening security crisis

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the top priority to tackle rising security threats? Stronger intelligence and prevention Better emergency response 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan's security forces are increasingly facing a deadly challenge as militant groups adopt a "double tap" strategy that turns rescue missions into ambushes. The tactic, analysed by Pakistani newspaper Dawn, involves an initial attack on a police or security installation, followed by a second strike targeting reinforcements rushing to the scene.The evolving strategy has coincided with a sharp rise in militant violence, particularly in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where police and military personnel have repeatedly come under attack in recent months. The latest assault came on Sunday, when a suicide bomber struck outside a police station in Swat's Kabal town during an anti-terror rally, killing at least 14 people, including police personnel, and injuring 18 others.According to an analysis by Dawn, militants have refined their tactics by carrying out coordinated two-stage attacks aimed at inflicting the highest possible casualties on responding security forces.The first team attacks a police station, checkpost or security installation, drawing personnel into a firefight. Simultaneously, another militant group positions itself along likely reinforcement routes.As additional police or military teams rush to assist, they are targeted through improvised explosive devices (IEDs), roadside ambushes or quadcopters capable of dropping explosives.Dawn said predictable response patterns have repeatedly turned reinforcement teams into easy targets. Over the past three years, at least 16 police personnel, including three deputy superintendents of police (DSPs), have been killed while responding to attacks rather than during the initial assault.The newspaper pointed to the July 29 attack in Hangu district as the latest example. Terrorists first stormed a police checkpost before attacking the reinforcements sent to support officers already under fire. Nine police personnel, including DSP Diyar Khan, were killed and 28 others injured. According to Dawn, it was the third major incident in which the second phase of the attack caused the heaviest losses.The pattern dates back to January 2023, when DSP Sardar Hussain and two of his guards were killed in an IED blast while responding to an attack on the Sarband police station near Peshawar.The strategy has unfolded alongside a broader escalation in militant attacks across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.On July 24, at least 15 people, including 14 security personnel, were killed after Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) militants attacked a joint police checkpost in Tank district. According to Pakistan's military, the attackers first attempted to breach the facility but were repelled before ramming an explosives-laden vehicle into the perimeter wall, triggering a massive blast that destroyed much of the checkpost. Security forces said 15 militants were killed during the operation, while 12 soldiers, two policemen and a forest department official lost their lives.Sunday's suicide bombing in Swat further highlighted the deteriorating security environment. The attacker detonated explosives after police attempted to stop and search him outside the Kabal police station, according to Dawn. The blast occurred near a large public demonstration where residents had gathered to protest the resurgence of militancy and demand stronger state action.Speakers at the rally criticised authorities for failing to curb militant activity and urged the government to restore lasting peace in the valley, which was once cleared of insurgents after a major military operation but has seen renewed militant activity in recent months.Data cited by Dawn from the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies showed that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa recorded 154 terrorism-related deaths in July, more than double the 75 fatalities reported in June, underscoring the rapidly worsening security situation.
Article Summary: Pakistan's security forces are increasingly facing a deadly challenge. Militants adopt a 'double tap' strategy that turns rescue missions into ambushes. The tactic involves an initial attack on a police or security installation, followed by a second strike targeting reinforcements rushing to the scene.

Article Title: Peace rally in Pakistan rocked by suicide blast; 14 killed, 20 injured
Article Text:
The blast occurred near Kabal Chowk, where residents had assembled for the 'Olasi Pasoon' peace gathering

PTM condemns attack on peace gathering

Death toll rises as investigation begins

Attack shakes peace rally

Rising militant violence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Pakistani leaders condemn bombing

At least 14 people were killed and 20 others injured on Sunday when a suicide bomber struck outside the Kabal Police Station in Pakistan’s Swat district during a large public rally against terrorism, police officials said. The attacker detonated explosives after officers attempted to stop and search him at the entrance of the police station, triggering panic among hundreds of demonstrators gathered nearby.The blast occurred near Kabal Chowk, where residents had assembled for the “Olasi Pasoon” peace gathering to demand an end to the recent resurgence of militant violence in the Swat Valley.Soon after the bombing, PTM Momand said its social media team was launching a campaign condemning the attack on what it described as a peaceful gathering.“PTM socialMediaTeam is launching a campaign to condemn the horrific bomb blast that targeted Apeaceful gathering of ‘Olasi Pasoon’ in Swat. People who assembled to demand peace wr met with violence instead. Initial reports indicate at least seven pple killed #StopStateTerrorismInSwat,” the group posted on X.Swat police spokesperson Nasir Iqbal Karimi confirmed that 14 people had died in the explosion. Earlier, Swat Deputy Inspector General of Police Fida Hussain said seven people, including four police officers, had been killed and 20 injured, but the death toll was later revised upward.According to Swat District Police Officer Umar Khan, the bomber blew himself up after police personnel tried to search him at the station gate. He said security forces had cordoned off the area and launched an investigation to gather further evidence.The attack took place as the final speaker was addressing the gathering, causing widespread panic among those attending the rally. Rescue teams, police and local authorities rushed to the scene, and the injured were taken to Saidu Sharif Teaching Hospital for treatment. No group had claimed responsibility for the bombing by Sunday evening.Before the explosion, speakers at the rally had condemned the rise in militant activity and demanded that the government ensure lasting peace in the region. They said their movement had a single agenda, the restoration of peace and the elimination of terrorism from Swat.The speakers argued that maintaining law and order and eradicating terrorism were the responsibility of the state, and warned that continued insecurity could fuel broader public unrest. They also criticised the authorities for allegedly taking action against peaceful citizens while militants continued to operate in the mountainous areas of Swat.“Our children deserve education, and our families deserve to live in peace,” one speaker told the crowd.“We have witnessed years of bloodshed. Our mothers, sisters, and daughters have suffered immensely, and we do not want another generation of widows and orphans.”The bombing came amid a sharp increase in militant violence across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Earlier on Sunday, an improvised explosive device blast near the Peshawar-Islamabad motorway toll plaza injured two police officers in Peshawar. On 30 July, nine police officers were killed in an attack on a police checkpost in Hangu.According to the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, excluding the merged districts, recorded 154 terrorism-related deaths in July, compared with 75 in June, an increase of 105 per cent.Pakistan President Asif Ali Zardari expressed sorrow over the loss of life and called for a comprehensive investigation into the bombing. He directed the relevant authorities to provide the best medical facilities to those injured.“Terrorists will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to harm peace, national unity, and the writ of the state,” he said, adding that the sacrifices of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police were a “source of pride for the entire nation”.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa governor Faisal Karim Kundi also condemned the attack, saying, “Terrorists cannot demoralise the nation with cowardly attacks.”Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's chief minister Sohail Afridi sought a report from the provincial Inspector General of Police and offered condolences to the families of the victims. “The elements hostile to peace will never be allowed to succeed in their nefarious intentions,” he said.
Article Summary: Suicide bomber detonates explosives after officers attempted to stop and search him at the entrance of the police station. Blast occurred near Kabal Chowk, where residents had assembled for the 'Olasi Pasoon' peace gathering. No group had claimed responsibility for the bombing by Sunday evening.

Article Title: 'Double standards': Pakistan rejects UN report on civilian casualties in Afghanistan strikes
Article Text:
Pakistan denies UN report that documents civilian casualties in Afghanistan, calls it 'baseless'

What the UN documented

Pakistan disputes UN findings

Pakistan's wider counterterrorism campaign

Pakistan’s military has rejected a UN report documenting hundreds of civilian casualties from cross-border fighting with Afghanistan, saying its forces targeted only Pakistani Taliban hideouts and other militant infrastructure and carried out the strikes in self-defence.Pakistan’s military spokesman Lt Gen Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry on Friday dismissed the findings as “baseless” and said Pakistani forces had not deliberately targeted civilians during operations against the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which Islamabad accuses of carrying out attacks from bases in Afghanistan.Chaudhry said Pakistan’s military had targeted “hideouts and infrastructure” used by the TTP and that those killed in the strikes were militants. He said the operations were necessary to protect people in Pakistan from attacks originating across the border.The comments came after the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) documented 499 civilians killed and 1,216 injured in cross-border armed violence between Afghanistan and Pakistan from October 1, 2025, to June 30, 2026.The UNAMA paper covering the latest quarter recorded 399 civilian casualties between April 1 and June 30 — 57 deaths and 342 injuries.Among them were 40 women and 112 children, including 26 children who were killed. UNAMA said the leading causes of civilian harm were airstrikes and ground engagements, and attributed all the cross-border civilian casualties it documented during the period to Pakistani security forces.The heaviest toll in the April-June period came from Pakistani airstrikes on June 28 in Paktya, Paktika and Kunar provinces, according to UNAMA. The strikes killed 28 civilians and injured 189 others, the report said.In one incident in Paktya's Chamkani district, UNAMA said a Pakistani airstrike hit a three-storey civilian residence. Residents gathered to rescue people trapped beneath the rubble, but a second airstrike struck the same location about 20 minutes later, while rescue efforts were under way.Chaudhry questioned the UN and Amnesty International reports, arguing that they relied heavily on accounts from Afghans despite what he described as restrictions on freedom of expression under Taliban rule.He also accused the Taliban government of allowing militant groups to operate from Afghan territory and said rights organisations had failed to adequately document attacks carried out against Pakistan.“These are double standards,” Chaudhry said, questioning how often rights groups had documented civilian casualties from US-led coalition airstrikes during the earlier war in Afghanistan.Chaudhry said Pakistan had recorded 3,145 terrorism incidents since January and that 2,084 militants had been killed, while 819 Pakistanis, including soldiers, police personnel and civilians, had died.He said Pakistani security forces had conducted 40,348 intelligence-based operations across the country during the same period.According to Chaudhry, Afghanistan-based militants had also carried out 28 suicide attacks in Pakistan since January. He alleged that many of those involved were Afghan nationals or people linked to Afghan security structures, and claimed some suicide bombers had been recruited from among drug users.Pakistan has vowed to continue its counterterrorism campaign, with Chaudhry saying the military would maintain operations against the TTP and affiliated groups.“We will continue these operations,” he said, adding that Pakistan was winning the fight against terrorism and would, “God willing”, win.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s military spokesman Lt Gen Ahmad Sharif Chaudhry dismissed the findings as ‘baseless’ He said Pakistani forces had not deliberately targeted civilians during operations against the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which Islamabad accuses of carrying out attacks from bases in Afghanistan.

Article Title: Rescuers find Nirmal Purja's body; all 10 climbers confirmed dead after avalanche on Broad Peak in PoK
Article Text:
Ten climbers, including Nirmal Purja, died in a Broad Peak avalanche. Search efforts continue for the remaining bodies after the incident.

Poll Vote & Share your view In your opinion, should documentaries about climbers and expeditions be more prevalent? Yes, they inspire others No, they glamorize risks 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Renowned British-Nepali mountaineer Nirmal Purja and nine other climbers swept away by an avalanche on PoK's Broad Peak have been confirmed dead, according to the Alpine Club of Pakistan and Purja's expedition company.Search and rescue teams are continuing efforts to recover the remaining bodies.The 10-member expedition was hit by an avalanche on Thursday while climbing Broad Peak in PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan region. Rescuers recovered three bodies on Friday after locating four, but harsh weather disrupted helicopter operations and delayed the search. Military-backed rescue teams resumed operations on Saturday."The world has lost one of mountaineering's greatest climbers," Purja's expedition company, Elite Exped, said in a statement. It added, "No words can ease the pain of this unimaginable loss."Confirming the tragedy, Alpine Club of Pakistan president Irfan Arshad Khan said, "The loss of these courageous climbers, who came from different nations united by their passion for the mountains, is an immeasurable loss to the global mountaineering fraternity."Paying tribute to rescuers, Khan said, "The mountains inspire us with their beauty, but they also remind us of the immense risks faced by those who venture into the high Himalaya and Karakoram."Earlier on Saturday, local police official Tahir Khan said the remains of Omani climber Nathira Ahmed were being flown to Islamabad, while the bodies of American climber Mallory Geis and Nepalese climber Bahadur Gurung remained at a hospital in Skardu.In a statement, Geis' family said, "Mallory was a bright light who was loved deeply by her family and friends. She will be profoundly missed."Purja, popularly known as Nims Dai, was a Nepal-born former British Army soldier who became one of the world's most celebrated mountaineers after scaling all 14 peaks above 8,000 metres in a record 189 days in 2019. The feat was documented in the Netflix film 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible. His record was surpassed in 2023.Describing Purja's legacy, Elite Exped said he was "a leader who inspired millions through his courage, humility and unwavering belief that human potential is far greater than we often imagine."The expedition marked Geis' first attempt at an 8,000-metre peak in PoK. It was also expected to be the final expedition for climber and guide Sakhi, who was also a geographer and high-altitude photographer, according to the Moving Mountains website.PoK's northern mountain ranges, including the Karakoram, are among the world's most challenging climbing destinations. Avalanches, falling ice and rocks, extreme altitude and rapidly changing weather frequently contribute to fatal accidents during expeditions.
Article Summary: The 10-member expedition was hit by an avalanche on Thursday while climbing Broad Peak in PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan region. Rescuers recovered three bodies on Friday after locating four, but harsh weather disrupted helicopter operations and delayed the search. Purja, popularly known as Nims Dai, was a Nepal-born former British Army soldier.

Article Title: Burnt-out vehicles, rock-strewn roads, heavy security: PoK votes in second phase amid unrest
Article Text:
The elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (PoK) have been overshadowed by violence, allegations of electoral rigging and reports of enforced disappearances

Heavy security, protests overshadow polling

India rejects PoK polls

Poll Vote & Share your view Should India take a more active role in opposing the elections in PoK? Yes, definitely No, it's not necessary 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan conducted the second phase of legislative assembly elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) on Sunday amid fresh unrest, with residents reporting burnt vehicles, rock-strewn roads and heavy security across parts of Muzaffarabad following clashes between protesters and security forces.The voting is taking place in the second of three phases for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly. However, the polls have been overshadowed by nearly two months of protests, allegations of election irregularities, political boycotts and a security crackdown.Residents of Muzaffarabad said fresh violence ahead of polling had raised concerns that the unrest would dominate the election process. Local reports described burnt-out vehicles, roads blocked with rocks and a strong presence of police, paramilitary personnel and army troops in several areas after clashes between demonstrators and security forces.Pakistan has deployed a three-tier security arrangement across PoK, with police, Pakistan Rangers, the Federal Constabulary and around 2,100 army personnel guarding polling stations.The elections come against the backdrop of sustained protests led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding greater political freedoms, economic reforms and the abolition of 12 assembly seats reserved for Pakistan-based refugees.The group has also sought better healthcare, education, employment opportunities and reduced political privileges.JAAC has boycotted the elections, arguing that the reserved refugee seats allow Pakistan's mainstream political parties to influence government formation in the region.The protest movement has intensified in recent weeks after talks with the authorities collapsed, leading to large demonstrations, strikes and clashes. Polling in two constituencies was postponed because of the deteriorating security situation.Rights groups, including the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, the United Nations and Amnesty International, have criticised the crackdown on protesters, internet restrictions and the ban imposed on JAAC under anti-terrorism laws.India has rejected the elections, describing them as a 'cosmetic' exercise aimed at legitimising Pakistan's 'illegal occupation' of the region.External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the entire Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, including areas under Pakistan's control are an integral part of India.He said the elections were an attempt by Pakistan to 'camouflage its illegal occupation' and conceal alleged human rights violations in the region."The current cosmetic electoral exercise is nothing but an attempt by Pakistan to camouflage its illegal occupation and hide its grave human rights violations in the region. The ongoing mass protest in the Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir is the direct consequence of its economic exploitation, its denial of fundamental rights to the people and its administrative oppression," Jaiswal had said earlier this week.
Article Summary: Pakistan conducted the second phase of legislative assembly elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) on Sunday. Residents reported burnt vehicles, rock-strewn roads and heavy security across parts of Muzaffarabad. The voting is taking place in the second of three phases for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly. The polls have been overshadowed by nearly two months of protests, allegations of election irregularities, political boycotts and a security crackdown.

Article Title: ‘Cockroaches’ and crackdowns: Can Pakistan’s Gen Z storm the barricades?
Article Text:
Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Asim Munir

The warning from within

A year-wise snapshot of terror attacks in Pakistan, with 2025 recording the highest number in more than a decade.

The uniform behind the curtain

A country of fragmented rebellions

A terrorised society

The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranks Pakistan as the country most affected by terrorism among 163 nations.

Where is Imran Khan now?

Beaten into submission

What’s next

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you support a unified movement from Gen Z in Pakistan? Absolutely Probably not 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Just look at what is happening in Pakistan -occupied Kashmir. People have taken to the streets over bread-and-butter issues and local election grievances. At least 40 protesters have died this week alone. To add insult to injury, Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif has described these protesters as “enemies” like India and ruled out dialogue with them."Its absolute disdain for the innocent people of PoK was laid bare when the defence minister branded the protesting civilians as enemies," external affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said. He said the “so-called” elections represented a “humiliating rejection” of the Pakistani establishment. "We urge that the international community should scrutinise Pakistan's actions and hold it accountable for its atrocities," Jaiswal added.And yet, the violence has barely registered internationally. Some foreign media outlets have offered customary coverage, often with the expected tilt, but it has largely been treated as business as usual in Pakistan. No professional outrage merchants or loud global campaigners have mounted a sustained protest against the conduct of the Pakistani army.Expectations from Pakistan are now so low that even the use of lethal force against its own people struggles to move the global news cycle.That silence says plenty about how the world views Pakistan. But the more interesting question is how Pakistanis see these protests themselves.Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi may have inadvertently supplied part of the answer.“Whether you agree or not, the system we have been living under has collapsed,” Naqvi said at event.But his most revealing remark came when he talked about Gen Z. “If these ‘Cockroaches’ get united, they can turn everything upside down,” Naqvi said.With around 60% of its population under 30 and an estimated 65-70 million people belonging to Gen Z, Pakistan appears, on paper, primed for a youth revolt. So why hasn’t Pakistan produced a nationwide Gen Z movement?Pakistan is a “hybrid regime”, as its own commentators describe it. Over the past two years, the army has moved beyond being informally supreme and begun formalising its dominance. A constitutional amendment created the post of chief of defence forces for the army chief, placing the navy and air force under him as well. His tenure was extended, and he was elevated to field marshal with what amounts to lifetime immunity from prosecution.None of this required a coup. It was delivered through a compliant civilian coalition of the PML-N and PPP that increasingly resembles the administrative wing of military rule rather than an elected government.The real genius of the military’s political arrangement has been its creation of an endless game of musical chairs. When one civilian face becomes unpopular, the establishment replaces it with another: the PPP, the Sharifs, Imran Khan , and then back again.This constant rotation serves a specific purpose. It prevents public anger from consolidating into a single grievance against the military establishment. Responsibility is repeatedly shifted to the civilian face of the day. When things go wrong, the answer offered is not structural change but another saviour, another party and another election promising to fix everything.For Gen Z, therefore, there is no clean and accessible target around which a national protest movement can form. A young Pakistani can be angry with a leader or political party. But the military, the country’s true centre of power, remains officially apolitical and practically beyond reach.Pakistan does not lack dissent. Its dissent is fragmented by geography, ideology and competing objectives.In Balochistan, the Baloch Liberation Army and its supporters are waging a separatist insurgency. The Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan is not fighting for democratic accountability; it seeks the imposition of Sharia law and the overthrow of the constitutional order. A Baloch nationalist, a TTP sympathiser and a university student in Lahore or Karachi protesting unemployment are unlikely to assemble beneath one banner or chant the same slogans.The state, therefore, does not need to defeat one unified movement. It only needs to prevent several incompatible movements from recognising that they are confronting the same power structure.That fragmentation also allows the establishment to treat every form of dissent differently: terrorism in one province, separatism in another, political disorder elsewhere and foreign conspiracy almost everywhere.Then there is the grim reality that Pakistan has become one of the world’s most terror-ravaged countries. The Global Terrorism Index 2026 ranked it as the country most affected by terrorism. Pakistan recorded over 1,000 terror-related deaths in 2025, its worst figures since 2013.This security crisis gives the army both political legitimacy and operational cover. Terrorism becomes the justification for an expanded military role, while dissent can be blurred with insurgency or branded “anti-state”. Extraordinary force is presented as an unavoidable response to extraordinary danger.The repression is often brutal but bureaucratically administered: Sedition cases, enforced disappearances, media blackouts, internet restrictions and the permanent threat of being labelled a traitor.Pakistan’s Gen Z has already seen what happens when a genuinely popular political leader crosses the establishment.For many young and urban Pakistanis, Imran Khan became a vehicle for expressing anger against a closed political system. His removal from power and the crackdown that followed offered a textbook lesson in the cost of direct confrontation.Look at where Khan is now. The hybrid regime is actively trying to neutralise the country’s most internationally recognisable political figure. If the establishment can do that to Imran Khan, what chance does an ordinary young Pakistani believe he has?If it comes to its survival, the regime would not mind killing even thousands.Reports of enforced disappearances and extrajudicial killings of Baloch and Pashtun activists surface with alarming regularity. Students, political workers, journalists and human rights defenders are reported missing after alleged abductions. Some are later found dead, their bodies bearing signs of torture.Pakistan’s own commission of inquiry documented more than 10,000 cases of enforced disappearance between 2011 and early 2024.For young Baloch and Pashtuns, the message could hardly be clearer: Challenging the state may result not merely in arrest, but in disappearance.This explains why Pakistan may not witness a Gen Z uprising in the classic sense: Millions occupying the streets, facing down the state and forcing a negotiated reset.Naqvi is right about one thing: if Pakistan’s young people unite, they could turn the system upside down. That is precisely why the system has spent decades ensuring they remain divided, disillusioned and afraid.Elsewhere, Gen Z has taken to the streets to reclaim its future from misrule. In Pakistan, it is being taught that survival itself may be the most it can hope for.
Article Summary: Pakistan is a ‘hybrid regime’, as its own commentators describe it. With around 60% of its population under 30 and an estimated 65-70 million people belonging to Gen Z, Pakistan appears, on paper, primed for a youth revolt. So why hasn't Pakistan produced a nationwide Gen Z movement?

Article Title: ‘Dhurandhar’ gangster’s brother shot in Karachi
Article Text:
Personal enmity or gang war? Probe on into hit on Zubair Baloch

Zubair Baloch — the brother of jailed Pakistan gangster Uzair Baloch, whose ruthless ascent was dramatised in the movie ‘Dhurandhar’ — is learned to be critically wounded following a targeted drive-by shooting in Karachi’s Lyari neighbourhood on Thursday evening, reports .The 40-year-old was sitting outside his Singu Lane home when two masked assailants on a motorcycle opened fire, striking him in the chest and abdomen.Zubair was rushed to Civil Hospital Karachi for emergency surgery. Two bystanders were also injured in the crossfire, with one reported to be in serious condition.According to Pakistan police, the attackers fled after a nearby shopkeeper returned fire. CCTV footage from the spot, which surfaced on Telegram channels, showed chaos on the street as the gunmen escaped.Police told the local press they were probing angles of personal enmity and the potential resurgence of long-standing gang wars.Zubair, arrested in multiple criminal cases in 2012, was released from prison last year, while his brother Uzair remains in jail serving a 12-year sentence handed down by a military court.Uzair and several accomplices were indicted for a 2012 armed attack on law enforcement officers under Kalakot police station’s jurisdiction.In April 2020, Uzair Baloch received a 12-year prison sentence for espionage.For decades, the historic Karachi neighbourhood of Lyari served as the epicentre of a gang war and a hub of organised crime. The turmoil traces back to early turf battles over drug trade routes and extortion rackets, which eventually expanded into a high-stakes proxy war involving major political factions.Notorious figures such as Sardar Abdul Rehman Baloch aka Rehman Dakait and his fierce rival Arshad Pappu turned narrow alleyways into battlegrounds, leveraging strategic political patronage through outfits like Peoples’ Aman Committee to insulate their syndicates from police oversight. Following Rehman Dakait’s death in a 2009 police encounter, his cousin Uzair Baloch stepped in to control the dominant faction.
Article Summary: Zubair Baloch, 40, was shot in the chest and abdomen on Thursday evening. He was sitting outside his home when two masked assailants opened fire. Two bystanders were also injured in the crossfire, with one reported to be in serious condition. Police are probing angles of personal enmity and the potential resurgence of gang wars.

Article Title: Pakistan minister invokes 'cockroaches' analogy, says united Gen-Z can 'turn everything upside down'
Article Text:
Calls for new provinces and decentralisation

'Biggest supporter' of democracy

Youth want jobs, not handouts

'Cockroaches' remark

Business community urged to back reforms

Mounting debt concerns

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for the youth? Merit-based jobs Welfare schemes Internships and training programs 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi on Thursday declared that the country's governance system had "collapsed", calling for the creation of new administrative units or provinces and urging political parties to reach a consensus on sweeping constitutional and governance reforms. He warned that without structural changes, Pakistan would remain trapped in recurring political and economic crises.Addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 in Islamabad, Naqvi said Pakistan's decades-old governance model had failed to deliver justice, economic opportunities or effective public services. He argued that decentralisation and the emergence of new leadership were essential to reform the country."Whether you agree or not, the system we have been living under has collapsed."Naqvi said repeated attempts to fix Pakistan's problems within the existing framework had failed, adding that the same debates would continue even a decade later unless the country's governance structure was fundamentally reformed."I believe the people responsible for bringing Pakistan to its current state are sitting in this hall," he said, adding that if a system had failed to function effectively for 70 to 80 years, there must be fundamental flaws in its design.The interior minister said the solution lay in decentralising governance through the creation of additional administrative units or provinces, arguing that local ownership would improve governance and allow new political leadership to emerge."The solution is only one.""You will have to take [the matter of] administrative units, provinces or whatever you may call it, to the public.""Unless units are made and they take ownership, and a new leadership comes, this will not happen."Naqvi urged all political parties to negotiate a comprehensive reform agenda instead of continuing with what he described as an outdated governance structure."All political parties should sit together in a single room, whether for a day, a month or a year. They will have to settle every issue of their country, including new units and provinces.""Unless they do so, unless they sit together and change this, this country will remain in the same condition, regardless of how many seminars and functions you hold."While describing himself as "the biggest supporter" of democracy, Naqvi argued that democratic governance could take different institutional forms and said Pakistan should not remain tied to a system that had consistently underperformed."We all want democracy. I am the biggest supporter of democracy and will remain so. But there are five or six systems within democracy. Yet we insist that no matter what happens, we must continue dragging along the same one."He also criticised policy failures, saying Pakistan continued to import agricultural commodities such as wheat despite being an agricultural country.Naqvi acknowledged the long working hours of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif but argued that the government remained focused on crisis management instead of long-term reforms."I have seen Shehbaz Sharif work 12 to 14 hours a day. He could even work 18 hours a day, but we are only firefighting.""Until you correct the basics of this country while adhering to the spirit of democracy, this will remain the same."Naqvi said Pakistan's young people were demanding merit-based employment, transparent recruitment and equal opportunities rather than welfare schemes or financial assistance."We think giving youngsters stipends of a few thousand rupees a month or tablets will make them happy, but ask them what they really want.""Their only demand is merit-based jobs and employment opportunities. They are not asking you for tablets or a few thousand rupees every month."According to the minister, Pakistani youth had the potential to earn between $2,000 and $4,000 per month if provided with the right opportunities.Referring to a term that has recently been used for Gen-Z in the wake of student protests in India, Naqvi warned that growing frustration among young people should not be ignored."If these 'Cockroaches' get united, they can turn everything upside down."He said the government should address the aspirations of young people before dissatisfaction intensified, arguing that their primary demands centred on merit-based jobs and equal opportunities.Naqvi also called on Pakistan's business community to play a more active role in reforming the country's political system, arguing that industrialists and traders had long been intertwined with politics."One gives funding of Rs500 million before elections, or the other gives Rs100 million or Rs50 million."He questioned why business leaders preferred financing political candidates instead of contesting elections themselves."Why don't businessmen enter politics? You are willing to fund politicians, but consider entering politics yourselves to be something shameful. You will have to stand up for yourselves."Highlighting Pakistan's fiscal challenges, Naqvi likened the federal government's finances to a household beginning every month already burdened with debt."The condition of this federal government is such that we make our budgets in the negative, and we discuss how much debt we have to incur this year.""[...] We will take more debts, but we will not correct things."He said leaders across the political spectrum understood the country's structural problems but had repeatedly failed to implement reforms, urging all stakeholders to build consensus on a long-term governance overhaul.
Article Summary: Mohsin Naqvi says Pakistan's governance system has "collapsed" Calls for creation of new administrative units or provinces. Urges political parties to reach consensus on constitutional and governance reforms. Calls on business community to play more active role in reforming the country.

Article Title: 34 killed as methane explosion tears through coal mine in Pakistan's Balochistan
Article Text:
Coal mine blast in Pakistan's Balochistan (AP photo)

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the compensation offered to families of miners is sufficient? Yes, it's fair No, it’s inadequate 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least 34 miners in Pakistan were killed and 10 other remained trapped after a methane gas explosion ripped through a coal mine in Balochistan province on Thursday, as officials told news agency AP.While rescuers continued a race against time to reach those still underground.The explosion took place on the outskirts of Quetta, the provincial capital, and was apparently triggered by a buildup of methane gas, according to government mine inspector Ghani Baloch.Rescue teams initially recovered the bodies of seven miners before locating 25 more, provincial officials and the disaster management agency said in a statement. The search and rescue operation was continuing as teams worked to locate and recover the remaining trapped workers.Baloch said rescue efforts would continue until all those trapped were accounted for, but warned that the death toll was likely to rise.“The chances of finding anyone alive diminish after methane gas explosions because oxygen levels drop to zero, and rescuers are also proceeding cautiously inside the mine,” Baloch said.Authorities have begun handing over the recovered bodies to their families for burial, while relatives of the missing miners continued to wait anxiously for updates, Baloch added.Balochistan's minister for mines and minerals Shoaib Nosherwani said rescue personnel were operating under extremely challenging conditions.Nosherwani expressed condolences to the victims' families and announced that the provincial government would provide compensation of 500,000 Pakistani rupees (about $1,800) to the family of each miner killed in the blast.He said authorities would conduct a thorough investigation into the cause of the explosion and review mining safety measures to prevent similar incidents.Meanwhile, the Pakistan Central Mines Labour Federation alleged that negligence may have contributed to the disaster. In a statement, the union urged the government to strictly enforce mining safety regulations and take stringent action against companies that violate mine safety laws.Fatal accidents are frequent in Pakistan's coal mining industry, particularly in Balochistan, where many mines operate without adequate ventilation, gas monitoring systems or other essential safety measures.Labour groups and mine workers have repeatedly accused mine owners of ignoring safety standards and failing to provide proper protective equipment.Despite the hazardous working conditions and meagre wages, thousands of people continue to rely on coal mining for their livelihoods in Balochistan, Pakistan's largest yet least developed province, where poverty and unemployment remain widespread.
Article Summary: The explosion took place on the outskirts of Quetta, the provincial capital, and was apparently triggered by a buildup of methane gas. Rescue teams initially recovered the bodies of seven miners before locating 25 more. The search and rescue operation was continuing as teams worked to locate and recover the remaining trapped workers.

Article Title: 11 police personnel, 15 militants killed in overnight attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (ANI file photo)

Pakistan suffered a major overnight militant attack on a police post in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, leaving 11 police personnel and 15 attackers dead by early Thursday.The attack targeted the Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire, police official Irfan Khan said.No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has intensified attacks on Pakistani security forces in the border region in recent months.The dead included police officer Diyar Khan, who was leading a reinforcement team to the attacked outpost, according to a statement from the provincial police. More than two dozen police personnel were also injured in the fighting.Police said the militants used heavy weapons to storm the post. Reinforcements heading to the scene were ambushed on the way, with an armoured personnel carrier damaged before officers regrouped and engaged the attackers, eventually forcing them back.Pakistan has seen a steady rise in militant violence in recent years, with the TTP blamed for many of the attacks. Although the group is separate from Afghanistan's ruling Taliban. Since the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021, Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Afghan government of sheltering TTP militants, a charge that Kabul has consistently denied.
Article Summary: Attack targeted Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)

Article Title: 'Frustration of their failure': Ex-envoy Vidya Bhushan Soni slams Pakistan over PoK unrest
Article Text:
Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (ANI file photo)

NEW DELHI: As unrest intensified in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) during the region's ongoing elections, former Indian envoy to Ukraine Vidya Bhushan Soni said the protests reflected growing frustration among people over Pakistan's failure to address its economic and domestic challenges.His remarks came after Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif called people in PoK as "enemies like India".Speaking to news agency ANI, Soni said frustration was growing in Pakistan because the country had expected to benefit by projecting itself as a mediator in international affairs and hoped that would help it secure economic assistance. "I think again there is a frustration creeping in, in Pakistan. Because they thought that they were playing the mediator role and they thought things would be fine and they would be once again back into business in terms of getting some economic aid, etc. That's not happening," he said.Soni said several groups opposed to the Pakistani government, including Baloch groups and people in PoK, were now putting pressure on Islamabad because they believed the country had reached a difficult position. According to him, Pakistan was more focused on projecting itself internationally as a peaceful nation than solving the problems of its own people."They are the ones who feel that we must put the pressure because now Pakistan is pushed to the wall.And so that's why they are coming out on the street; they are showing their frustration, they're showing their anger, they're showing their patience is running thin," he said.He added that Pakistan should first address the concerns of its own citizens instead of trying to play a larger role on the global stage. "You have to do something about the people, their own people, rather than trying to go and solve the world's problem; first you solve your own problem back home," Soni said.Warning that the unrest was unlikely to end anytime soon, Soni alleged that Pakistan could respond by using force against its own people because its priorities remained focused on international issues. "It has consequences; it will not stop because Pakistan's priority still continues to be international, and they will try to come down heavily through the use of force on their own people," he said.Calling the situation in PoK particularly worrying, Soni said many residents felt their grievances were being ignored, which had deepened their frustration. "The worrisome factor right now is POK because they have seen that their case is not being heard; they are totally ignored. So I feel that it's a frustration of their failure," he said.Meanwhile, the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKAAC), through a series of posts on X, raised concerns over the treatment of injured people and the presence of masked individuals in civilian clothing alongside police personnel during the crackdown. "The treatment of the injured and the presence of masked individuals in civilian clothing alongside police officers raise serious concerns that require urgent scrutiny," the group said.The committee also alleged that civilian property had been damaged during the operation, saying, "The destruction of civilian property raises serious concerns about the conduct of the security forces during the ongoing crackdown." It further claimed that surveillance equipment had been deliberately destroyed, adding, "The deliberate destruction of surveillance equipment raises serious concerns about transparency, accountability, and the preservation of evidence. "Calling for international attention, the JKAAC urged the United Nations, international media, diplomatic missions and human rights organisations to examine the footage from the clashes and launch an independent probe. "We call on the United Nations, international media, diplomatic missions, and international human rights organisations to examine this footage, independently verify the facts, and support an immediate, independent and impartial international investigation into the recent events in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir," the group said.
Article Summary: Former Indian envoy to Ukraine Vidya Bhushan Soni says protests reflect Pakistan's failure to address its economic and domestic challenges. Soni said frustration was growing in Pakistan because the country had expected to benefit by projecting itself as a mediator in international affairs. Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif called people in PoK as "enemies like India"

Article Title: Is Pakistan facilitating Chinese missile shipments to Iran? Islamabad responds
Article Text:
Pakistan army chief Asim Munir (AP file photo)

Pakistan has pushed back strongly against reports claiming it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran, as Tehran remains locked in a tense standoff with the Donald Trump-led US administration.The rejection by Munir's military comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington, exposing its two-faced tendency in its foreign policy approach.Pakistan’s military chief has recently found favour with US President Donald Trump , while Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.Reacting to reports that Pakistan was set to facilitate the transit of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air defence missile systems to Iran, the Trump's "favourite field marshal"-led army dismissed the claims outright.“All such speculations are baseless and devoid of truth,” Pakistan’s military media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said, according to Azerbaijan news, citing Anadolu Agency.“Such speculations are categorically rejected,” the ISPR added.The denial came after Reuters reported on Wednesday that Iran was expected to receive its first shipment of Chinese air defence systems within weeks, as Tehran looks to rebuild its defensive capabilities amid its conflict with the United States.According to Reuters, the initial deliveries were planned to move from Urumqi in western China and pass through Pakistan before reaching Iran, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. The sources, however, did not clarify whether the transit would take place by air or through land routes.The reports emerged amid speculation over US weapons stockpiles being stretched due to ongoing global conflicts, though Trump later dismissed such concerns. The episode has once again highlighted Islamabad’s delicate balancing act between Beijing and Washington as tensions continue to rise around Iran.
Article Summary: Pakistan denies reports it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran. Comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington. Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.

Article Title: Security forces’ crackdown, civil unrest continue in POK, 20 dead
Article Text:
File photo: PoK unrest

The situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir ( POK ) remains volatile amid mass civilian unrest, election-related violence, and heavy crackdowns by Pakistani security forces. According to sources, Pakistani forces used lethal force against Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) during their long march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad.The crackdown reportedly resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left over 33 protesters injured.Amnesty International USA said that the disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot were consistent with Pakistani authorities’ “long history of unlawful violence against protesters”. “We urge the Pakistani authorities torestore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area,” it said.While security forces continue to maintain a heightened presence in Rawalakot, Muzaffarabad and other areas, sources said the possibility of additional protests remains high over the coming days because of declining public confidence in the political process.Local authorities have also continued to impose communication blackouts and suspended services across POK.
Article Summary: Pakistani forces used lethal force against Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) during their long march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad. The crackdown reportedly resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left over 33 protesters injured. Local authorities have also continued to impose communication blackouts and suspended services across POK.
